modules.title: What Is Philosophy
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 1 of Humanities for Technologists. I'm your instructor, and over the next fourteen modules we're going to build the disciplines of judgment that turn a capable builder into a senior technologist — someone whose decisions deserve trust. We start at the root: this module maps the branches of philosophy and shows how each one already lives in your technical work — logic in code, ethics in deployment, epistemology in science, aesthetics in design.
objectives: Name the major branches of philosophy and their questions
Connect each branch to a concrete technical practice
Distinguish philosophy from science and from opinion
Read a philosophical argument charitably before criticizing it

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Your working vocabulary for the whole course — every term below returns in later modules.
- **logic** — the study of valid reasoning; lives in type systems and formal verification.
- **epistemology** — the theory of knowledge: what it is, where it comes from, its limits; lives in experiment design and the replication crisis.
- **metaphysics** — the study of what exists.
- **ethics** — the study of right action; lives in every deployment decision.
- **aesthetics** — the study of beauty and taste; lives in API and interface design.
- **political philosophy** — the study of justice and power.
- **applied branches** — philosophy of science, philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, and philosophy of technology apply the core branches to domains (philosophy of mind, for instance, to debates about machine intelligence).
- **argument** — premises plus an inference leading to a conclusion; a philosophical claim stands or falls on its argument.
- **principle of charity** — reconstruct the strongest version of a position before attacking it; the correct response to a supported claim is to engage its premises or its inference.
- **opinion vs. argument** — "that's just your opinion" is a category error when the claim is backed by reasons.
- **the technologist's failure mode** — optimization without direction: precise answers to the wrong questions. Technical training teaches how to build; the humanities teach what building is *for*. Philosophy supplies the questions.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Branch-map your own work — thirty minutes, pen and paper or a blank document.
1. **List three recent technical decisions** you made or watched (a schema choice, a deploy approval, an experiment design).
2. **Assign each a branch.** Which was really a logic question (validity of the reasoning)? An epistemology question (what the data establishes)? An ethics question (who it affects)? An aesthetics question (clarity of the interface)?
3. **Extract one argument.** Take the most contested decision and write it as premises → inference → conclusion.
4. **Apply charity.** Rewrite the opposing position in its strongest form before you critique it — no straw men allowed.
5. **Name the missing question.** For each decision, write the question philosophy would have asked that the technical discussion skipped. That list is your study agenda for this course.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a one-page Branches Audit of a live project.** Pick a system you work on. For each of the six branches — logic, epistemology, metaphysics (what the system's data model claims exists), ethics, aesthetics, political philosophy (who holds power over the system) — write two sentences on where that branch's questions show up in the project. Close with one paragraph: which branch's questions is your team currently ignoring, and what is that neglect costing? This audit becomes your personal map for the rest of the course — revisit it in Module 14.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what does the principle of charity require before you criticize a design proposal?
- Give Noah three technical practices and name the branch behind each: (a) a type-system rule, (b) an A/B test design, (c) a deployment-approval gate.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to sketch (in text) the anatomy of an argument — premises, inference, conclusion — using one of your own recent decisions as the example."
- *Honesty:* ideas in this course are paraphrased and attributed to their traditions — no quotation is fabricated, and nothing here is legal, financial, or professional advice.

cards.front: Name four traditional branches of philosophy and each one's central question.
cards.back: Logic (valid reasoning), epistemology (what is knowledge?), metaphysics (what exists?), ethics (what is right action?).

cards.front: What is the principle of charity?
cards.back: Reconstruct the strongest version of an opposing position before criticizing it.

cards.front: How does a philosophical claim differ from a mere opinion?
cards.back: It is backed by an argument — premises and inference that can be evaluated.

cards.front: Give one technical practice shaped by each: logic, epistemology, ethics.
cards.back: Logic: type systems/verification. Epistemology: experiment design. Ethics: deployment decisions.

cards.front: What is the failure mode of pure technique, and what does philosophy supply?
cards.back: Optimization without direction — precise answers to the wrong questions. Philosophy supplies the questions.

cards.front: Metaphysics, aesthetics, political philosophy: the central question of each?
cards.back: Metaphysics: what exists? Aesthetics: what is beauty and taste? Political philosophy: what is justice, and who holds power?

cards.front: Philosophy of mind: two central questions, and why a technologist cares?
cards.back: What is consciousness — does a system that behaves intelligently actually understand? And the mind–body problem — how do mental states relate to physical ones? Technologists meet these in machine-intelligence debates: whether a model 'understands' or merely simulates is a philosophy-of-mind question, and the answer shapes how we evaluate and trust systems. (See Concepts; quiz item 3.)

cards.front: Name two technical practices philosophy shaped, with the branch behind each.
cards.back: Formal logic → computation and verification: valid inference underpins proof assistants and type systems. Epistemology → the experimental method and statistics: what counts as knowing shapes hypothesis testing, significance, and replication. A third: ethics → professional codes and AI-safety governance. (See Concepts.)

quiz.q: Which branch asks 'What can we know?'
quiz.explain: Epistemology is the theory of knowledge — its nature, sources, and limits. (See 'Concepts': epistemology.)

quiz.q: The principle of charity requires:
quiz.explain: Charity means engaging the strongest form of the argument, not a weak caricature. (See 'Concepts': principle of charity.)

quiz.q: Philosophy of mind is most relevant to which technical debate?
quiz.explain: Questions about what minds are — and whether machines could have them — are philosophy of mind. (See 'Concepts': applied branches.)

quiz.q: An argument consists of:
quiz.explain: The logical structure: premises support the conclusion via an inference. (See 'Concepts': argument.)

quiz.q: The metaphysical question most relevant to a digital-twin project is:
choices: What exists, and what is real versus simulated?
quiz.explain: Metaphysics asks what exists; a digital twin forces the question of what counts as real — its state, its identity over time. (Concepts: metaphysics.)

quiz.q: A teammate says 'that view is just relativism — everything goes.' The charitable first move is:
choices: Ask what precisely they mean by 'relativism' before evaluating
Label the fallacy and move on
Restate their position in the weakest possible form
quiz.explain: Charity reconstructs the strongest version first; 'everything goes' is likely a straw version of their claim. (Concepts: principle of charity.)

quiz.q: Which pairing is correct?
choices: Epistemology — the study of valid reasoning
Logic — the study of what we can know
Aesthetics — the study of beauty and taste
quiz.explain: Logic studies valid reasoning; epistemology studies knowledge; aesthetics studies beauty and taste; metaphysics studies what exists. (Concepts: the branches.)

quiz.q: The module's 'failure mode of pure technique' is:
choices: Solving precisely framed problems while ignoring whether the framing is right
quiz.explain: Technique optimizes within a frame; philosophy interrogates the frame — the goals, the categories, what is excluded. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Logic & Argumentation
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 2. I'm your instructor, and this is the module that sharpens every other one: deductive validity, inductive strength, and the classic fallacies. By the end you'll be able to take any claim from a spec, a paper, or a meeting — extract its argument, test its form, and spot the fallacies hiding in technical discourse.
objectives: Test an argument for deductive validity
Distinguish deduction from induction and abduction
Identify the common informal fallacies
Spot fallacies in technical discourse

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The toolkit for evaluating claims — learn the names, then use them on your own arguments first.
- **deductive argument** — an argument whose conclusion is claimed to follow necessarily from its premises.
- **valid** — a deductive argument is valid if the conclusion *must* be true whenever the premises are; validity is about form, not content.
- **sound** — valid *and* with premises that are actually true.
- **modus ponens** — if P then Q; P; therefore Q.
- **modus tollens** — if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
- **induction** — generalization from instances ("every tested build passed, so the suite is green"); strong but never certain.
- **abduction** — inference to the best explanation ("the outage pattern matches a DNS failure"); the logic of debugging.
- **ad hominem** — attacking the person instead of the argument.
- **straw man** — refuting a distorted version of a position.
- **appeal to authority** — citing status instead of reasons ("no senior engineer would design it that way").
- **false dilemma** — presenting two options when more exist ("we either rewrite everything or accept the outage").
- **post hoc** — "after, therefore because of" ("the deploy caused the bug because it came first").
- **begging the question** — smuggling the conclusion into a premise.
- **slippery slope** — asserting an unargued chain of consequences.
- **the naming caveat** — naming a fallacy is the start of the reply, not the whole reply; you still owe the substantive counterargument. Confusing deduction, induction, and abduction is a constant source of overclaiming.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Dissect a live technical argument — do this on a real claim from your work this week.
1. **Capture a claim.** Take one contested claim from a recent spec, review, or meeting — verbatim.
2. **Extract the argument.** Write its premises and conclusion explicitly. If you can't find the premises, the claim is running on implication — flag that.
3. **Classify the inference.** Deduction, induction, or abduction? Apply the right standard: validity for deduction, strength of evidence for induction, best-explanation fit for abduction.
4. **Test validity.** If deductive, check the form — does the conclusion follow even if you disagree with the premises?
5. **Test soundness.** Are the premises actually true? One false premise sinks soundness even with perfect form.
6. **Scan for fallacies.** Run the classic list: ad hominem, straw man, authority, false dilemma, post hoc, question-begging, slippery slope.
7. **Charitable rewrite.** Reconstruct the strongest version of the argument, then write your reply to *that*.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a one-week fallacy log.** For five working days, log every informal fallacy you spot in meetings, docs, and chat — the verbatim claim, the fallacy name, and a one-line charitable rewrite of what the speaker should have argued. Minimum ten entries. Close with a half-page reflection: which fallacy does your own team commit most, and what process change would catch it? (Naming the fallacy never substitutes for the substantive reply — the log must include your counterargument for each entry.)

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what is the difference between a valid argument and a sound one?
- Give Noah three workplace claims and name the fallacy: (a) "no senior engineer would design it that way", (b) "we either rewrite everything or accept the outage", (c) "the deploy caused the bug because it came first".
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to lay out a modus tollens for one of your debugging hypotheses: if the cache were stale we would see X; we do not see X; therefore…"
- *Honesty:* logic is a tool for evaluating arguments, not a weapon for winning meetings — apply the fallacy list to your own claims first.

cards.front: Valid vs sound argument?
cards.back: Valid: conclusion must follow if premises true. Sound: valid + premises actually true.

cards.front: Modus ponens and modus tollens?
cards.back: Ponens: P→Q, P ⊢ Q. Tollens: P→Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P.

cards.front: Deduction vs induction vs abduction?
cards.back: Deduction: certain, form-based. Induction: generalization from instances. Abduction: best-explanation inference.

cards.front: Define: straw man, false dilemma, post hoc.
cards.back: Straw man: attack a distortion. False dilemma: two options where more exist. Post hoc: after⇒because-of.

cards.front: Why is naming a fallacy not a complete rebuttal?
cards.back: You still owe the substantive counterargument — the label diagnoses, it doesn't refute by itself.

cards.front: Define: begging the question; appeal to authority.
cards.back: Begging the question (petitio principii): the conclusion is smuggled into a premise — the argument goes in a circle. Appeal to authority: accepting a claim because a prestigious source says so rather than because of evidence or reasoning. The module's CTO-Postgres example is an appeal to authority: the choice might be right, but the reason given is the wrong one. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Distinguish 'valid' from 'true', one sentence each.
cards.back: True is a property of propositions (they correspond to the facts). Valid is a property of arguments (the conclusion follows from the premises — the premises cannot be true while the conclusion is false). An argument can be valid with false premises, and a conclusion can be true while the argument for it is invalid. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Sketch a cogent inductive argument from operations.
cards.back: Inductive form: many observed instances → probably-general conclusion, strength graded by sample size, representativeness, and controls. Ops example: 'Of the last 40 deploys with this canary pattern, none caused an incident; so the next canary deploy is probably safe' — strong if the 40 are representative, weak if conditions changed. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: 'All servers are machines; db-1 is a server; therefore db-1 is a machine' is:
quiz.explain: Correct form (syllogism) with true premises — valid and sound. (See 'Concepts': valid, sound.)

quiz.q: 'Either we migrate now or the system collapses' — with no evidence of collapse — is:
quiz.explain: It asserts only two options without ruling out the rest — the false-dilemma pattern. (See 'Concepts': false dilemma.)

quiz.q: Inferring 'the cache is stale' as the best explanation of the symptoms is:
quiz.explain: Best-explanation inference from evidence — abduction, the logic of debugging. (See 'Concepts': abduction.)

quiz.q: 'The CTO prefers Postgres, so Postgres is the right choice' is:
quiz.explain: Status substitutes for reasons — the CTO's preference is not itself an argument. (See 'Concepts': appeal to authority.)

quiz.q: A sound argument requires premises that are:
choices: True, combined with a valid inference
quiz.explain: Sound = valid form + true premises. Persuasiveness is rhetoric, not logic. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Affirming the consequent — 'if the cache is stale the page is slow; the page is slow; so the cache is stale' — is:
choices: A formal fallacy: the consequent does not determine the antecedent
quiz.explain: A slow page has many possible causes; the form 'if P then Q; Q; therefore P' is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. Denying the consequent would be valid (modus tollens). (Concepts.)

quiz.q: In the Hands-on procedure, the 'steel-man' step asks you to:
choices: Find the strongest version of the opposing argument
Name every fallacy in the opponent's case
quiz.explain: Steel-manning is charity in practice: rebuild the opponent's case at its strongest before rebutting, so the rebuttal actually lands. (Hands-on procedure.)

quiz.q: Abductive reasoning is best described as inference to:
choices: The best explanation of the evidence
quiz.explain: Abduction proposes the hypothesis that best explains the observations — the daily bread of debugging and incident response. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Ethics I — The Three Traditions
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 3. I'm your instructor, and this is where judgment gets its frameworks: virtue ethics, deontology, and consequentialism — three traditions that answer 'what should I do?' with three different decision procedures. You'll apply all three to the same technical dilemma, and discover that their disagreements are the point.
objectives: State the core question of each tradition
Apply each to a technical dilemma
Compare how the three can disagree on one case
Recognize which tradition you default to

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Three traditions, three decision procedures — know what each asks before you need it under pressure.
- **virtue ethics** — asks not "what should I do?" but **"what kind of person should I be?"**; right action flows from cultivated virtues (honesty, courage, prudence, justice) developed by habit.
- **Aristotle** — *Nicomachean Ethics* (4th c. BCE); the good life as *eudaimonia*, flourishing through virtuous activity. Engineering analogue: the craftsperson's character — care, honesty about limits, refusal to cut corners.
- **deontology** — duty-based: some acts are required or forbidden regardless of consequences.
- **Kant** — the **categorical imperative** (*Groundwork*, 1785): (1) act only on maxims you could will as universal law; (2) treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. Engineering analogue: duties not to deceive users, not to ship known-harmful systems, respect for autonomy — even when breaking them would "work better".
- **consequentialism** — judge acts by their **outcomes**; the right act maximizes good consequences.
- **utilitarianism** — the classical form (Bentham, Mill, 18th–19th c.): maximize overall happiness/well-being. Engineering analogue: cost-benefit analysis, risk assessment, expected-value reasoning.
- **each tradition's vulnerability** — virtue: vague guidance in hard cases. Deontology: rigid; duties can conflict. Consequentialism: can justify sacrificing individuals for the aggregate, and demands consequence-predictions we rarely can make.
- **one case, three verdicts** — shipping an addictive-engagement feature: the virtue ethicist asks whether it expresses the character of a good craftsperson; the deontologist asks whether it treats users as mere means; the utilitarian weighs aggregate engagement-happiness against aggregate harm. The traditions can and do disagree — that disagreement is the point of studying all three.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the three-traditions analysis on a real decision you are facing or recently made.
1. **State the decision** in one sentence, naming the action you are actually considering.
2. **Virtue pass.** Ask: what would the good craftsperson do here? Which virtues (honesty, care, courage) are exercised or betrayed?
3. **Deontology pass.** Ask: could I will everyone in my position to do this? Does it treat any person merely as a means?
4. **Consequentialist pass.** Ask: what are the expected aggregate outcomes — including second-order effects and the worst plausible case?
5. **Compare verdicts.** Where the traditions agree, decide with confidence. Where they disagree, write down exactly what the disagreement is about — that sentence is the real decision.
6. **Document.** File the analysis with the decision; your future self (or your reviewer) deserves the reasoning, not just the outcome.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a two-page ethics review memo.** Take a real product decision — past or pending — and run all three traditions on it, following the Hands-on procedure. The memo must contain: the decision stated plainly, each tradition's analysis in its own section, the point of disagreement, and your recommendation with reasons. If all three traditions agree, say so and say why the case was easy; if they split, own the split.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what question does each tradition ask? (Virtue: what kind of person should I be? Deontology: what is my duty? Consequentialism: which act has the best outcomes?)
- Give Noah the addictive-engagement feature and ask which tradition condemns it fastest — and on what grounds.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to lay out the three verdicts side by side for a deploy decision you are facing, then point to where they disagree."
- *Honesty:* these frameworks structure judgment; they do not automate it — a memo that cites a tradition without doing the analysis is ethics theater.

cards.front: Virtue ethics: core question and key figure?
cards.back: 'What kind of person should I be?' — Aristotle; virtues cultivated by habit.

cards.front: Kant's categorical imperative (two formulations)?
cards.back: Act only on universalizable maxims; treat humanity as an end, never merely as a means.

cards.front: Utilitarianism: core claim and key figures?
cards.back: Right act maximizes overall well-being — Bentham, Mill.

cards.front: Each tradition's main vulnerability?
cards.back: Virtue: vague guidance. Deontology: rigid, conflicting duties. Consequentialism: justifies sacrificing individuals; needs impossible predictions.

cards.front: State the decision procedure of each tradition in one line.
cards.back: Virtue: what would the good craftsperson do? Deontology: could I will this as universal law, and does it treat persons as ends? Utilitarianism: which act maximizes expected good outcomes?

cards.front: The three verdicts on an addictive-engagement feature — one line each?
cards.back: Virtue: does it express a good craftsperson's character? Deontology: does it treat users as mere means? Utilitarian: do aggregate harms outweigh engagement-happiness?

cards.front: State the trolley problem's function in ethics teaching.
cards.back: It isolates the clash between traditions: the utilitarian pulls the lever (minimize deaths); the Kantian objects (using the one as a mere means is forbidden regardless of outcome); the virtue ethicist asks what a person of practical wisdom would do. Its value is diagnostic, not decisive — it reveals which considerations your judgment actually weighs. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is 'moral luck', and why does it matter for engineers?
cards.back: Moral luck: outcomes beyond our control (which deploy hits production at 3 AM, which bug ships on a Friday) affect blame and praise. Engineers feel it acutely: identical diligence can produce a quiet quarter or a sev-1. Judge decisions by the quality of the process and foreseeable risk, not by how the dice landed. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: 'Would I endorse everyone doing this?' is the decision procedure of:
quiz.explain: Universalizability is Kant's test — the first formulation of the categorical imperative. (See 'Concepts': Kant, categorical imperative.)

quiz.q: A utilitarian evaluates shipping a risky feature by:
quiz.explain: Consequentialism judges by outcomes — expected benefits weighed against expected harms. (See 'Concepts': consequentialism.)

quiz.q: Aristotle's term for flourishing through virtuous activity?
quiz.explain: Eudaimonia — often translated flourishing — is the telos of the virtuous life. (Arete is virtue/excellence itself.) (See 'Concepts': Aristotle.)

quiz.q: Treating users 'merely as means' would be condemned by:
quiz.explain: The humanity formulation: never treat rational agents merely as instruments. (See 'Concepts': categorical imperative.)

quiz.q: Virtue ethics locates moral quality primarily in:
quiz.explain: Virtue ethics asks 'what kind of person acts this way?' — character, cultivated by habit, aiming at flourishing (eudaimonia). (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A team ships a feature knowing 1% of users will be harmed but 99% helped, with no way to target. A Kantian objects because:
choices: The 1% are being used as mere means to others' ends
quiz.explain: Kant's humanity formulation forbids treating persons merely as means — the end does not justify using people. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: 'The greatest good for the greatest number' is the slogan of:
quiz.explain: Classical utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill): maximize aggregate well-being. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Rule utilitarianism differs from act utilitarianism in that it evaluates:
choices: The general rule the act instantiates, for its tendency to maximize good
quiz.explain: Rule utilitarians judge the rule ('do engineers keep their promises?') rather than each act in isolation — a move that answers some classic objections. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Ethics II — Technology & Responsibility
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 4. I'm your instructor. Last module gave you the three traditions; this one puts them to work where you live — applied ethics for builders. Dual use, the Collingridge dilemma, responsibility gaps, and professional codes: by the end you'll know who answers when systems cause harm, and what to do before they do.
objectives: Explain the Collingridge dilemma
Analyze a dual-use technology case
Locate responsibility in a sociotechnical system
Use a professional code as a decision input, not an oracle

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
From theory to the systems you ship — the applied vocabulary.
- **Collingridge dilemma** — David Collingridge (1980): early in a technology's life we can shape it but cannot know its consequences; late, we know the consequences but the technology is entrenched and hard to change. Implication: design that is anticipatory, reversible, and humble rather than confidently predictive.
- **dual use** — technologies serving benign and harmful ends with the same mechanism: cryptography, drones, facial recognition, large language models, gene editing. Resists two lazy answers — "technology is neutral" (it isn't; affordances shape use) and "ban it all" (which forfeits the benefits). The serious question is always *which uses, under what controls*.
- **responsibility gap** — in sociotechnical systems, harm can emerge with no single responsible agent; designers, deployers, users, and institutions each hold a piece.
- **the engineer's four moves** — **document** foreseeable misuses, **build in** friction against the worst ones, **instrument** for monitoring, and **preserve** human override. "The model did it" is not an excuse a professional can offer.
- **professional codes** — the ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct (updated 2018) and the IEEE Code of Ethics state duties: avoid harm, be honest, respect privacy, honor confidentiality. Codes do not decide hard cases — they set the floor and give you language to escalate with. Know your profession's code; cite it when you push back.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Dual-use audit of a system you touch — do this on something real.
1. **Name the core mechanism** of your system in one sentence — what it does, mechanically.
2. **List benign uses** — who benefits, and how.
3. **List harmful uses of the same mechanism** — be specific and concrete; vagueness here is the evasion.
4. **Apply the four moves.** For each harmful use: what would you document, what friction would you build in, what would you instrument, where does a human keep override?
5. **Write the misuse section** of your design doc or README — foreseeable misuses, controls, and residual risks, in plain language.
6. **Cite your code.** Note which clause of the ACM or IEEE code your analysis rests on, so the escalation has standing.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a responsible-deployment plan.** For a system you own (or the resume-screening case from this course's scenarios), produce: (a) the dual-use analysis, (b) the four moves implemented as concrete controls, (c) the monitoring that would catch misuse, (d) the rollback and reversibility story per Collingridge. If the honest conclusion is "do not ship", the plan says so — with the traditions from Module 3 cited.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what is the Collingridge dilemma — and what design stance does it imply?
- Give Noah two technologies and ask for the dual-use read: (a) facial recognition, (b) an open-source vision library — which uses, under what controls?
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to sketch the responsibility map — designer, deployer, user, institution — and mark where each of your four moves lands."
- *Honesty:* document your reasoning as if a court, a regulator, and your future self will all read it — because each of them might.

cards.front: The Collingridge dilemma?
cards.back: Early: we can shape tech but can't foresee consequences. Late: we foresee but can't reshape — entrenchment.

cards.front: What is dual use?
cards.back: One technology serving benign and harmful ends (crypto, drones, facial recognition, LLMs).

cards.front: The responsibility gap?
cards.back: Harm emerges from a sociotechnical system with no single responsible agent.

cards.front: The engineer's four moves against foreseeable misuse?
cards.back: Document misuses, build in friction, instrument for monitoring, preserve human override.

cards.front: What are professional codes for (ACM 2018)?
cards.back: A floor and a shared language for escalation — not an oracle for hard cases.

cards.front: Give two dual-use examples from the module and the governance question each raises.
cards.back: Facial recognition: security and convenience versus mass surveillance — who controls the watchlist? Large language models: productivity versus automated phishing and disinformation — whose misuse counts as foreseeable? The governance question is always: which uses do we enable by default, and who decides? (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is 'ethics washing'?
cards.back: Adopting the language and theater of ethics — principles pages, advisory boards with no power — without changing incentives, metrics, or shipped behavior. The module's test: if the ethics review can stop a launch, it is governance; if it only decorates one, it is washing. (Concepts.)

cards.front: State the 'foreseeable misuse' standard and its limit.
cards.back: Engineers are responsible for misuses a competent professional could foresee — not for every imaginable abuse. The limit matters: responsibility scales with foreseeability and with your power to mitigate, not with perfect prediction. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The Collingridge dilemma implies designers should favor:
quiz.explain: Since early knowledge is poor and late change is hard, keep options open and design for reversibility. (See 'Concepts': Collingridge dilemma.)

quiz.q: Facial recognition is best described as:
quiz.explain: Same mechanism serves security/authentication and mass surveillance — the question is which uses under what controls. (See 'Concepts': dual use.)

quiz.q: 'The model did it' as a defense fails because:
choices: Professionals retain responsibility for foreseeable system behavior
quiz.explain: Professional responsibility covers foreseeable misuse of systems you design and deploy. (See 'Concepts': the engineer's four moves.)

quiz.q: The ACM Code of Ethics (2018) is best used as:
choices: A decision oracle for hard cases
A floor and shared language for escalation
quiz.explain: Codes set minimums and give practitioners vocabulary to raise concerns — they don't automate judgment. (See 'Concepts': professional codes.)

quiz.q: An engineer discovers the recommendation system amplifies self-harm content. The module's first move is:
choices: Quietly patch the ranking and say nothing
Document the finding, escalate through the proper channel, and propose a fix
quiz.explain: Document and escalate through the code's channels: it creates the record, engages the right decision-makers, and preserves the engineer's leverage. (Hands-on procedure.)

quiz.q: 'We can always add ethics later, once we have users' is most directly challenged by:
quiz.explain: Collingridge: early on we can change the technology but don't know the harms; later we know the harms but the technology is entrenched. 'Later' is exactly when change is hardest. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The responsibility gap arises when:
choices: An autonomous system's decisions cannot be attributed to any human's intent or control
quiz.explain: The gap: the system acts, harm follows, but no human foresaw, intended, or controlled the specific decision — so traditional responsibility finds no foothold. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A professional code of ethics functions best as:
choices: A floor and shared language for escalation
quiz.explain: Codes give engineers words and backing when they raise concerns — a floor below which practice must not sink, not an oracle for hard cases. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Epistemology & Philosophy of Science
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 5. I'm your instructor, and this module is about the authority science claims and how it earns it: what counts as knowledge, Popper's falsifiability, Kuhn's paradigms — and why all of it matters the next time you design an experiment, read a paper, or trust a metric.
objectives: State the classic JTB account of knowledge and its problem
Explain falsifiability and why it matters
Describe Kuhn's account of scientific revolutions
Apply these ideas to experiment design and the replication crisis

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
How knowledge claims earn (or fail to earn) your trust.
- **knowledge (JTB)** — the classic account: S *knows* p iff p is true, S believes p, and S is *justified* in believing p.
- **Gettier problem** — Gettier's 1963 counterexamples showed justified-true-belief can be accidentally true; the practical residue: belief + truth isn't enough — the *route* to the belief matters.
- **falsifiability** — Karl Popper (*The Logic of Scientific Discovery*, 1934): science advances by **conjecture and refutation**; a theory is scientific insofar as it **forbids some possible observations**. "This model explains everything" is not praise — an unfalsifiable claim cannot be tested.
- **paradigm** — Thomas Kuhn (*The Structure of Scientific Revolutions*, 1962): science alternates between **normal science** (puzzle-solving inside a paradigm) and **revolutionary** episodes where anomalies accumulate and the paradigm is replaced — Copernican, Newtonian, Einsteinian, quantum. Paradigms shape what counts as a legitimate question, which is why revolutions feel like world-changes.
- **replication crisis** — across psychology, medicine, and ML-adjacent fields, landmark findings failed to replicate — driven by **p-hacking**, **publication bias**, and low power.
- **the remedies** — **pre-registration**, replication, and **meta-analysis**: how a field earns the title of knowledge. Treat every striking result as a conjecture awaiting refutation.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Falsify your own claim before anyone else does — run this on your current most impressive result.
1. **Write the striking claim** — a metric improvement, a model result, a performance assertion.
2. **List its falsifiers.** What observations would prove it wrong? If you can't name any, the claim is unfalsifiable — restate it until it forbids something.
3. **Audit the route.** Could p-hacking, cherry-picked splits, or selection of only the good runs have produced this result?
4. **Pre-register.** Write the hypothesis, the metric, the analysis, and the decision rule *before* you run the next test — then run it.
5. **Seek replication.** Have someone else reproduce it, or reproduce it on fresh data. One unreplicated result is a conjecture, not knowledge.
6. **Report uncertainty.** Effect size with uncertainty beats a bare "significant" — and say what would change your mind.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a replication-ready experiment plan.** One page: the claim, its falsification criteria, the pre-registered analysis, the sample and data plan, and the replication step. Then run it — and file the result whether it confirms or refutes. A refuted conjecture, documented, is worth more than an untested "win".

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what makes a theory scientific for Popper?
- Give Noah two claims and ask which is falsifiable: (a) "this model explains all failures", (b) "disabling the cache raises p99 above 200ms".
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to draw the Kuhn cycle — normal science → anomaly → crisis → revolution → new normal — and place your field's last big shift on it."
- *Honesty:* treat every striking result as conjecture awaiting refutation — including your own, especially your own.

cards.front: JTB account of knowledge?
cards.back: S knows p iff p is true, S believes p, S is justified — challenged by Gettier cases (1963).

cards.front: Popper's demarcation criterion?
cards.back: Falsifiability: a scientific theory must forbid some possible observations.

cards.front: Kuhn's normal vs revolutionary science?
cards.back: Normal: puzzle-solving within a paradigm. Revolutionary: paradigm replacement after anomaly accumulation.

cards.front: Name two drivers of the replication crisis and two remedies.
cards.back: Drivers: p-hacking, publication bias, low power. Remedies: pre-registration, replication, meta-analysis.

cards.front: Why is 'explains everything' not praise for a theory?
cards.back: An unfalsifiable theory forbids nothing, so no observation can test it — Popper's point.

cards.front: State the problem of induction in one paragraph.
cards.back: Hume's challenge: no finite run of observations logically entails that the next will conform. We assume nature is uniform — the future resembles the past — but that assumption cannot be proven without circularity. Science does not solve this; it works around it with probabilistic reasoning, replication, and models that quantify uncertainty. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Bayesian vs. frequentist probability — the one-line contrast.
cards.back: Frequentist: probability is long-run frequency of repeatable events. Bayesian: probability is a degree of belief, updated by evidence via Bayes' rule. The practical point: Bayesian thinking formalizes 'how much should this evidence move my prior?' — the daily question of incident triage and A/B testing. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is a 'crucial experiment'? Give one.
cards.back: An experiment whose outcome decisively favors one theory over a rival. Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition: Einstein predicted starlight would bend near the sun by a specific amount; the measured deflection matched Einstein, not Newton — a crucial result for general relativity. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A theory compatible with every possible observation is, for Popper:
quiz.explain: Falsifiability is the demarcation line: no forbidden observations, no science. (See 'Concepts': falsifiability.)

quiz.q: Gettier cases show that:
choices: Justified true belief can be accidentally true
quiz.explain: Gettier constructed JTB cases where the belief is true by luck — intuitively not knowledge. (See 'Concepts': Gettier problem.)

quiz.q: In Kuhn's account, a paradigm determines:
choices: What counts as a legitimate problem and solution
quiz.explain: Paradigms structure normal science — its questions, methods, and standards of success. (See 'Concepts': paradigm.)

quiz.q: Pre-registration primarily combats:
quiz.explain: Locking in hypotheses and analyses before seeing data removes the garden of forking paths. (See 'Concepts': the remedies — pre-registration.)

quiz.q: In the JTB account, Gettier cases are counterexamples to the claim that:
choices: Justified true belief is sufficient for knowledge
quiz.explain: Gettier showed one can have justified true belief by luck — the belief is true but not knowledge — so JTB is not sufficient. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Falsifiability, for Popper, is a criterion of:
quiz.explain: A theory is scientific if it forbids some possible observation — it can be proven wrong. Compatible-with-everything theories are not science, whatever their truth. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A p-value of 0.04 means:
choices: There is a 4% chance the hypothesis is false
Assuming the null hypothesis, results this extreme occur 4% of the time
quiz.explain: The p-value is conditional on the null — it is not the probability the hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about effect size or replicability. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Kuhn's 'incommensurability' claim is that rival paradigms:
choices: Cannot be compared by any neutral standard
quiz.explain: Competing paradigms see different problems, use terms differently, and lack a neutral court of appeal — which is why revolutions involve persuasion, not just proof. (Concepts.)

modules.title: History of Science I — Antiquity to Newton
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 6. I'm your instructor. We now turn to context — the story of how systematic knowledge of nature became possible, from Babylonian star records to Newton's synthesis. This is History of Science I: antiquity to Newton, and the instruments and mathematics in between.
objectives: Name key figures and their contributions through 1700
Explain what made the Scientific Revolution revolutionary
Describe the mathematization of nature
Connect early instruments to early theories

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The figures and ideas that built the method — dates are load-bearing; learn them.
- **Babylonians** (by ~700 BCE) — systematic astronomical records and base-60 arithmetic still in our clocks.
- **Euclid's *Elements*** (~300 BCE) — the **axiomatic method**: definitions, postulates, proof — the template for rigorous mathematics ever since.
- **Archimedes** (3rd c. BCE) — buoyancy, levers, approximations of pi by inscribed polygons: theory married to machines.
- **Ptolemy's *Almagest*** (2nd c. CE) — planetary motion modeled with **epicycles**: wrong in structure, superb in prediction, dominant for 1400 years.
- **Islamic Golden Age** (8th–13th c.) — preservation and extension of Greek science: **Al-Khwarizmi** (algebra — his name gives us "algorithm"), **Ibn al-Haytham** (optics and an early experimental method).
- **Copernicus** (1543) — moved the sun to the center.
- **Kepler** (1609–1619) — elliptical orbits and three laws, derived from Tycho Brahe's data.
- **Galileo** — telescope (1609), inclined-plane experiments; made motion mathematical; paid for heliocentrism with house arrest (1633).
- **Newton's *Principia*** (1687) — three laws of motion plus universal gravitation: one mathematics for falling apples and orbiting moons; co-inventor (with Leibniz) of the calculus.
- **the Revolution's method** — mathematized hypotheses tested against precise, often instrument-mediated measurement; the Newtonian program of reducing phenomena to mathematical law defined science for two centuries and still structures engineering education.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Reconstruct one link in the chain — pick a figure who is not Newton.
1. **Pick a figure** from this module's earlier centuries.
2. **State the prevailing view** they inherited, in its strongest form — charity applies to the past too.
3. **Name the anomaly or instrument** that broke it — whose data, which device.
4. **State the new claim** precisely, and name the mathematics that carried it.
5. **Name what it preserved.** Revolutions contain their past: what of the old view survived inside the new one?
6. **Draw the engineering moral.** Which of your own tools and theories are Ptolemaic epicycles — predictively strong but structurally wrong?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a "Long View" memo.** Trace one modern tool you use daily (your ML library's optimizer, your database's index, your clock's timekeeping) back through three historical layers to this module's period. One page: the modern tool, the 19th/20th-century science behind it, and the pre-1800 root. The point is not trivia — it is seeing your stack as the tip of a 2,700-year project.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what did the Scientific Revolution change methodologically?
- Give Noah three names and ask for the contribution: Euclid, Al-Khwarizmi, Kepler.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to sketch the timeline 700 BCE → 1687 with one line per figure — and mark where instruments start driving theory."
- *Honesty:* history is told from evidence, not nostalgia — attribute, date, and qualify. Ptolemy was wrong about structure and magnificent at prediction, and both facts matter.

cards.front: Euclid's Elements: contribution?
cards.back: The axiomatic method — definitions, postulates, theorems proved from them (~300 BCE).

cards.front: Al-Khwarizmi and Ibn al-Haytham: known for?
cards.back: Al-Khwarizmi: algebra ('algorithm'). Ibn al-Haytham: optics and early experimental method.

cards.front: Kepler's three laws (in brief)?
cards.back: Elliptical orbits (sun at focus); equal areas in equal times; T² ∝ a³.

cards.front: Newton's Principia (1687): the synthesis?
cards.back: Laws of motion + universal gravitation: one mathematics for terrestrial and celestial motion.

cards.front: What made the Scientific Revolution methodologically new?
cards.back: Mathematized hypotheses tested against precise, often instrument-mediated measurement.

cards.front: Thales to Aristotle: the one-sentence story of Greek natural philosophy.
cards.back: Thales (~600 BCE) proposed a single natural principle (water) behind appearances — explanation without gods. The atomists (Democritus) added indivisible particles in void. Aristotle then built the comprehensive system: four causes, natural place, teleology — brilliant, wrong in details, and dominant for two millennia. (Concepts.)

cards.front: The Islamic Golden Age: three contributions the module names.
cards.back: Ibn al-Haytham's optics: controlled experiments with light, an early scientific method (~1000 CE). Al-Khwarizmi's algebra: systematic equation-solving — the root of 'algorithm'. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad: preservation and extension of Greek astronomy and medicine. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Why does the module call dates 'load-bearing'?
cards.back: Dates anchor causal order: you cannot claim Newton 'responded to' Einstein, or alchemy 'failed because of' chemistry before chemistry existed. Load-bearing dates prevent anachronism — the most common failure mode in technical histories of ideas. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Ptolemy's Almagest is best described as:
choices: A geocentric model, predictively strong for 1400 years
quiz.explain: Epicycles were structurally wrong but predicted planetary positions well — a lesson in prediction vs. truth. (See 'Concepts': Ptolemy's Almagest.)

quiz.q: The word 'algorithm' derives from:
quiz.explain: The 9th-century scholar's name, Latinized, attached to his systematic procedures. (See 'Concepts': Al-Khwarizmi.)

quiz.q: Galileo's 1633 condemnation concerned:
quiz.explain: The Inquisition's trial centered on his defense of the Copernican system. (See 'Concepts': Galileo.)

quiz.q: Kepler derived his laws primarily from:
quiz.explain: Brahe's unprecedentedly precise naked-eye data made the ellipses detectable. (See 'Concepts': Kepler.)

quiz.q: Aristotle's physics was wrong about projectile motion mainly because:
choices: It relied on teleology and natural place rather than inertia
quiz.explain: Aristotelian physics explained motion by purposes and natural places; inertia — motion continuing without a mover — was the conceptual break. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The Library of Alexandria's significance for science was:
choices: It proved the Earth was flat
It concentrated texts, instruments, and scholars — enabling Eratosthenes' measurement of Earth's circumference
quiz.explain: Eratosthenes (~240 BCE) measured Earth's circumference to within a few percent using shadows at two locations — possible because the Library gathered the data and the geometry. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Copernicus's De revolutionibus (1543) is best described as:
choices: A mathematical reformulation, initially read as a calculating device, that later generations turned into cosmology
A refutation of Ptolemy by new observation
quiz.explain: Copernicus offered a heliocentric model largely for mathematical elegance; Osiander's preface even framed it as a fiction. The revolution was what Kepler, Galileo, and Newton made of it. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The printing press mattered to the Scientific Revolution because it:
choices: Let results, tables, and diagrams circulate identically — enabling cumulative, checkable science
quiz.explain: Identical copies meant distant readers could check the same figure and data — the material basis of cumulative science. (Concepts.)

modules.title: History of Science II — 1800 to the Present
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 7. I'm your instructor. Last module ended with Newton; this one covers the two centuries that built the modern world — energy, evolution, electromagnetism, relativity, quantum theory, and computation. History of Science II: 1800 to the present.
objectives: Trace the major 19th–20th century revolutions
Explain the significance of Maxwell, Darwin, Einstein, and the quantum founders
Describe the birth of computing
Connect scientific revolutions to engineering practice

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Two centuries of revolutions — and the pattern they share.
- **thermodynamics** — Carnot, Clausius, Kelvin: energy conservation and **entropy**; the science of engines became the science of everything.
- **Darwin** — *On the Origin of Species* (1859): **natural selection** explains adaptation without design.
- **Maxwell** (1860s) — four equations unifying electricity, magnetism, and light; predicting electromagnetic waves, confirmed by Hertz (1887).
- **Planck** (1900) — quantized energy to solve blackbody radiation.
- **Einstein** — 1905 (photoelectric effect, special relativity; the "miracle year" also covered Brownian motion and atoms) and 1915 (general relativity): rewrote space, time, and gravity.
- **the quantum founders** — Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Dirac (1920s): quantum mechanics, probabilistic at its core, technologically the foundation of semiconductors and lasers.
- **Turing** (1936) — the **universal machine**: computation's theoretical foundation, before any general-purpose computer existed.
- **Shannon** (1948) — **information theory**: bits, channel capacity, the mathematics of communication.
- **theory into infrastructure** — ENIAC (1945), the transistor (1947), integrated circuits (1958), ARPANET (1969): theory became infrastructure within a generation.
- **the pattern** — unification (Maxwell, Einstein), then mathematization, then instruments, then engineering. Each revolution preserved the old theory as a **limiting case** — Newton survives inside Einstein at low speeds. Science grows by *containing* its past, not erasing it.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Map one revolution end to end — Maxwell, Darwin, quantum, or computation.
1. **Pick a revolution** from this module.
2. **Name the two domains unified** (or the single orthodoxy overthrown).
3. **State the mathematics** that carried the new theory.
4. **Name the instrument or engineering** that followed — and how fast (years from theory to device).
5. **State the limiting case.** What does the old theory still correctly describe, and where does it break?
6. **Find the live analogue.** Which current orthodoxy in your field shows the same pre-revolution symptoms — anomalies accumulating, patches multiplying?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a two-page revolution case study.** Choose one: Maxwell's unification, the quantum revolution, or the birth of computation. Cover: the problem the old theory couldn't solve, the new mathematics, the confirming experiment or instrument, the engineering it enabled, and the limiting-case relationship. Close with one paragraph on what the case teaches about evaluating bold technical claims today.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, how do scientific revolutions relate to the theories they replace?
- Give Noah two dates and ask what happened: 1859, 1936.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to map the chain theory → instrument → infrastructure for one case — say, quantum theory → transistor → integrated circuits — with the dates."
- *Honesty:* dates and attributions are load-bearing in history — 1905 is not 1915, and Shannon is not Turing; precision is respect.

cards.front: Maxwell's achievement (1860s)?
cards.back: Unifying electricity, magnetism, and light in four equations; predicting EM waves.

cards.front: Darwin 1859: the mechanism?
cards.back: Natural selection — differential survival and reproduction of heritable variants.

cards.front: Einstein's 1905 'miracle year' outputs?
cards.back: Photoelectric effect (light quanta), special relativity, Brownian motion (atoms).

cards.front: Turing 1936 and Shannon 1948: contributions?
cards.back: Turing: the universal machine (computation theory). Shannon: information theory (bits, channel capacity).

cards.front: How do revolutions relate to old theories?
cards.back: The old theory survives as a limiting case — e.g., Newton inside Einstein at low speeds.

cards.front: The 1905 'miracle year': name the papers and their targets.
cards.back: Photoelectric effect (light quanta — the quantum seed), Brownian motion (atoms are real — the statistical proof), special relativity (space and time are not absolute), and E=mc² (mass–energy equivalence). One patent clerk, one year, four foundations. (Concepts.)

cards.front: The DNA double helix (1953): whose data, whose model?
cards.back: Franklin and Wilkins's X-ray diffraction (Photo 51) supplied the decisive structural data; Watson and Crick built the model that explained it. The module's lesson: credit follows the explanatory synthesis, but the synthesis needs the data — know both halves of the story. (Concepts.)

cards.front: How does the module say revolutions relate to old theories?
cards.back: New theories swallow the old as limiting cases: relativity reduces to Newton at low speeds, quantum mechanics to classical at large scales (the correspondence principle). Revolutions extend the domain of validity; they do not erase what worked. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Maxwell's equations unified:
quiz.explain: One framework for electric and magnetic fields, with light as an electromagnetic wave. (See 'Concepts': Maxwell.)

quiz.q: Hertz's 1887 experiments confirmed:
quiz.explain: Hertz generated and detected radio waves — the waves Maxwell's theory required. (See 'Concepts': Maxwell, Hertz.)

quiz.q: Turing's 1936 paper established:
choices: The theoretical model of universal computation
quiz.explain: The universal Turing machine defined computability before electronic computers existed. (See 'Concepts': Turing.)

quiz.q: The transistor (1947) rested on which science?
quiz.explain: Band theory and semiconductor physics are quantum-mechanical — 1920s theory, 1940s device. (See 'Concepts': the quantum founders; theory into infrastructure.)

quiz.q: Lavoisier's contribution to chemistry was to:
choices: Replace phlogiston with quantitative, mass-conserving chemistry
quiz.explain: Lavoisier's balance-sheet chemistry — mass is conserved in reactions — ended the phlogiston era and founded modern stoichiometry. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The Michelson–Morley experiment (1887) is famous for:
choices: Failing to detect the ether, clearing the path for relativity
Measuring the speed of light exactly
quiz.explain: The null result — no ether drift — was the anomaly that special relativity dissolved by removing the ether's job. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) showed, for formal arithmetic:
choices: Any consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove
quiz.explain: No consistent formal system proves its own consistency (second theorem) — limits on formalism from within formalism. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Plate tectonics was accepted in the 1960s mainly because of:
choices: Seafloor-spreading data and magnetic striping — a mechanism plus measurements
quiz.explain: Wegener had the pattern but no mechanism; magnetic stripes on the seafloor supplied both mechanism and measurement, and the field converted within a decade. (Concepts.)

modules.title: History of Technology
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 8. I'm your instructor. Science tells you what is true; this module tells you what *happens* — how technologies diffuse, why smart incumbents miss transitions, and what the industrial revolutions teach anyone building on a platform shift today.
objectives: Name the industrial revolutions and their core technologies
Explain technology diffusion and the S-curve
Describe why incumbents fail at transitions
Draw lessons for current platform shifts

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
How technologies actually spread — and who gets blindsided.
- **First Industrial Revolution** (~1760–1840) — steam, mechanized textiles, iron: Britain's factories.
- **Second Industrial Revolution** (~1870–1914) — electricity, steel, chemicals, the internal-combustion engine: mass production.
- **Third Industrial Revolution** (~1960s–) — electronics, computers, the internet: information as the factor of production.
- **Fourth** (claimed, from the 2010s) — cyber-physical systems, AI; historians differ on the count.
- **S-curve** — technologies diffuse along an S-curve: slow uptake, explosive growth, saturation. Infrastructure (railways, grids, fiber) determines the slope — technology without distribution is a demo.
- **Rogers' adopter categories** — innovators → early adopters → early majority → late majority → laggards.
- **Moore's chasm** — the gap between early adopters and the early majority; crossing it is the go-to-market crux.
- **Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma** (1997) — incumbents rationally serve their best customers with sustaining improvements, and are blindsided by **disruptive** technologies that start worse and cheaper, then climb the S-curve.
- **Kodak** — invented the digital camera (1975, Steve Sasson) and still lost; the dilemma is structural, not a failure of intelligence.
- **the internet's lesson** — ARPANET (1969) → TCP/IP standardization (1983) → the Web (1990–) → broadband → mobile: each layer enabled the next, and open protocols beat walled gardens at the infrastructure layer. Bet on open layers, expect the application layer to surprise you, and remember that distribution — not just invention — decides winners.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run a disruption self-assessment on your own product — answer in writing.
1. **Name your best customers** and the sustaining improvements you ship for them.
2. **Find the cheaper, worse entrant.** Who serves the customers you ignore, with something you'd be embarrassed to ship?
3. **Ask what job it does** for those overlooked customers — in their words, not yours.
4. **Place yourself on the S-curve.** Slow uptake, explosive middle, or saturation? What infrastructure sets your slope?
5. **Locate the chasm.** Are you selling to early adopters while the early majority waits for proof? What proof would they need?
6. **Write the incumbent's memo.** Draft the one-page warning your successor would write about you — then decide whether to act on it.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a two-page transition brief.** Pick a current platform shift (AI agents, edge compute, post-quantum cryptography — your choice). Cover: S-curve position with evidence, chasm status, the incumbent most at risk and why, the open layer to bet on. One recommendation, with the reasoning a skeptic would demand.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what is the Innovator's Dilemma — and why isn't it about stupidity?
- Give Noah two cases and ask for the disruption read: (a) Kodak and the digital camera, (b) open protocols versus walled gardens at the infrastructure layer.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to sketch the S-curve, mark the chasm, and place your product on it — then defend the placement."
- *Honesty:* the S-curve is a model, not a prophecy — it organizes evidence; it does not replace it.

cards.front: The three (or four) industrial revolutions and their cores?
cards.back: 1st: steam/textiles/iron. 2nd: electricity/steel/chemicals/engines. 3rd: electronics/computers/internet. 4th (claimed): cyber-physical/AI.

cards.front: The S-curve of diffusion?
cards.back: Slow start, explosive middle, saturation — adoption over time; infrastructure sets the slope.

cards.front: Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma (1997)?
cards.back: Incumbents rationally optimize for best customers and are disrupted from below by cheaper, initially-worse tech.

cards.front: Kodak and the digital camera?
cards.back: Kodak invented it (1975, Steve Sasson) yet lost — the dilemma is structural, not stupidity.

cards.front: The internet's architectural lesson?
cards.back: Open protocols won the infrastructure layer; each layer enabled the next; distribution decides.

cards.front: Name the four industrial revolutions and each one's core technology.
cards.back: 1st (~1760–1840): steam, mechanized textiles, iron. 2nd (~1870–1914): electricity, steel, chemicals, the assembly line. 3rd (~1960s on): electronics, computing, the internet. 4th (proposed): cyber-physical systems, AI, biotech — the module treats the label as contested, the technologies as real. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is 'technological momentum' (Hughes)?
cards.back: Hughes's middle path between determinism and free choice: young systems are shaped by society; mature, entrenched systems acquire momentum and start shaping society back — they develop mass, direction, and velocity. Think of the highway system, the power grid, or IPv4. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Give the module's account of why incumbents miss disruptions.
cards.back: Incumbents rationally serve their best customers with sustaining improvements; disruption starts in overlooked segments with 'worse' products that improve along a different trajectory. Kodak invented the digital camera (1975) but its business model needed film — the innovator's dilemma is a dilemma because both choices are locally rational. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The Second Industrial Revolution is associated with:
quiz.explain: ~1870–1914: electrification, Bessemer steel, chemical industry, internal combustion. (See 'Concepts': Second Industrial Revolution.)

quiz.q: Moore's 'chasm' lies between:
choices: Early adopters and the early majority
quiz.explain: Crossing from enthusiasts to the pragmatic majority is the go-to-market crux. (See 'Concepts': Moore's chasm.)

quiz.q: A disruptive technology, in Christensen's sense, typically starts:
choices: Worse and cheaper, serving overlooked customers
quiz.explain: Disruption enters low-end or new markets, then moves up as performance improves. (See 'Concepts': disruptive technologies.)

quiz.q: TCP/IP standardization (1983) mattered because:
choices: It created a common open layer enabling the internet's growth
quiz.explain: An open, shared protocol layer let diverse networks interoperate — infrastructure for everything above. (See 'Concepts': the internet's lesson.)

quiz.q: The First Industrial Revolution began in Britain partly because of:
choices: Coal, colonies, and capital — cheap energy plus investable surplus
quiz.explain: Accessible coal solved the energy bottleneck; colonial trade and financial institutions supplied capital. Technology needs its economic soil. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The Luddites (1811–1816) were protesting:
choices: The use of machinery to deskill labor and cut wages — a labor dispute, not technophobia
quiz.explain: 'Luddite' is misused as 'anti-technology'; the historical Luddites smashed frames as leverage in a wage dispute over deskilling. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Containerization (1950s) mattered because it:
choices: Standardized the interface between cargo, ships, and ports — collapsing handling costs and enabling globalization
quiz.explain: The box was an interface standard; the revolution was in the handling system around it — a lesson for every API designer. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The 'productivity paradox' (Solow, 1987) observed that:
choices: The computer age was visible everywhere except the productivity statistics
quiz.explain: Gains took decades to show in aggregate statistics — measurement lags, complementary reorganization, and the J-curve of general-purpose technologies. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Technical Writing
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 9. I'm your instructor, and this module is pure craft: technical writing as a professional discipline. Structure for scanners, precision over decoration, the core documents — and the editing pass where the real work happens.
objectives: Structure a document for scanning, not just reading
Write in active voice with concrete subjects
Define terms before using them
Produce documentation, RFCs, and status updates that get read

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The working rules of prose that gets read.
- **BLUF** — Bottom Line Up Front: put the **conclusion first**, then evidence; write for scanners, not just readers. A design doc's first paragraph should let a busy reader decide whether to read the rest.
- **active voice** — with concrete subjects: "The deploy script restarts the service" beats "The service is restarted."
- **define before use** — define every term before first use; never let "it", "this", or "thing" carry load.
- **numbers over adjectives** — "p99 latency rose from 40ms to 900ms" beats "latency got much worse."
- **no throat-clearing** — delete "It is important to note that…".
- **RFC / design doc** — problem, goals/non-goals, proposal, alternatives considered, risks, rollout.
- **runbook** — symptoms → diagnosis → fix; tested by someone who didn't write it, during calm — never first-tested in a real incident.
- **status update** — what changed, what's blocked, what's next: three bullets, no novel.
- **commit message** — what *and* why; the diff already shows the what.
- **editing is the work** — first drafts are for the writer; editing is for the reader. Cut 20% on the second pass as a discipline; read aloud to catch tangles. The standard: a competent stranger, interrupted twice, can still follow it. Strunk & White's *The Elements of Style* (1918): "omit needless words".

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Rewrite a real document you shipped — a design doc, an incident review, or a status update.
1. **Pick the document** — something with a real audience, not a draft.
2. **BLUF it.** Move the conclusion to paragraph one. If the document has no conclusion, write one — that's the diagnosis.
3. **Activate the voice.** Convert every passive to active with a concrete subject.
4. **Quantify.** Replace each adjective of degree ("much worse", "significantly") with a number.
5. **Cut 20%.** Delete throat-clearing, hedged restatements, and any sentence the document survives without.
6. **Read it aloud.** Tangles you hear are tangles your reader will trip on — untangle them.
7. **Hand it to a stranger.** A competent colleague who lacks your context reads it once, interrupted twice. Where they stall, rewrite.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a portfolio document set.** For a real project, produce three documents to this module's standard: (a) a one-page RFC/design doc with all six sections, (b) a runbook a stranger could execute, (c) a three-bullet status update. Each must survive the read-aloud test and the 20% cut. File them where your team will actually find them — a document nobody can find is a document you didn't write.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what does BLUF demand of your first paragraph?
- Give Noah three sentences and ask which is strongest: the passive, the active, and the throat-clearer.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to take one of your paragraphs and show the 20% cut inline — what goes, and why."
- *Honesty:* clarity is respect for the reader's time — and the standard is the interrupted stranger, not your own satisfaction.

cards.front: BLUF?
cards.back: Bottom Line Up Front — conclusion first, then evidence; write for scanners.

cards.front: Three rules of precise technical prose?
cards.back: Active voice with concrete subjects; define terms before use; numbers over adjectives.

cards.front: Sections of an RFC/design doc?
cards.back: Problem, goals/non-goals, proposal, alternatives considered, risks, rollout plan.

cards.front: What makes a good commit message?
cards.back: What AND why — the diff already shows the what.

cards.front: Strunk & White's core maxim?
cards.back: 'Omit needless words.' (The Elements of Style, 1918.)

cards.front: The inverted pyramid: structure and origin.
cards.back: Most important information first, then supporting detail, then background — so a reader who stops early still got the point. Borrowed from journalism; the module applies it to incident reports, design docs, and status updates. BLUF is its one-line form. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Active vs. passive voice: the module's actual rule.
cards.back: Not 'never passive' — prefer active for actions with a clear actor ('the deploy script deleted the table'); use passive when the actor is unknown or irrelevant ('the table was dropped at 03:14') or to keep the subject stable across sentences. The rule is precision, not dogma. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What belongs in a postmortem's 'Timeline' vs. 'Root cause' vs. 'Action items'?
cards.back: Timeline: what happened when, in UTC, with detection and mitigation timestamps — facts only. Root cause: the deepest fixable cause (five whys), stated without blame. Action items: each with an owner and a date — a postmortem without owned actions is a memoir. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Which sentence is strongest?
choices: The service is restarted by the script.
The deploy script restarts the service.
It is important to note the service gets restarted.
quiz.explain: Concrete subject, active verb, no throat-clearing. (See 'Concepts': active voice.)

quiz.q: BLUF means:
quiz.explain: Lead with the conclusion so scanners can triage. (See 'Concepts': BLUF.)

quiz.q: A runbook is tested by:
choices: Someone who didn't write it, during calm
quiz.explain: Only a fresh reader proves the runbook is self-sufficient; never first-test it in a real incident. (See 'Concepts': runbook.)

quiz.q: 'Latency got much worse' should become:
quiz.explain: Numbers beat adjectives — precise, checkable, actionable. (See 'Concepts': numbers over adjectives.)

quiz.q: The strongest revision of 'The thing was kind of slow sometimes' is:
choices: P99 latency exceeded the 800ms SLO on 12% of requests during peak
quiz.explain: Numbers, scope, and the standard violated — the sentence now supports a decision. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: In a design doc, 'Non-goals' exist to:
choices: Bound the proposal — stating what it deliberately will not do
quiz.explain: Explicit non-goals prevent scope creep in review and tell readers where the design's promises end. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The best test of a runbook is:
choices: That an on-call engineer who has never seen the system can execute it under pressure
quiz.explain: A runbook is tested by execution under cognitive load — the novice-on-call criterion. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: 'We should migrate' is weak because it lacks:
choices: An actor, an object, and a reason — who should do what, to what, and why
quiz.explain: Recommendations need agent, action, target, and rationale — otherwise nobody can approve or execute them. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Rhetoric & Persuasion
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 10. I'm your instructor. Writing gave you clarity; this module gives you movement — rhetoric, the honest craft of moving people with reasons. Ethos, pathos, logos; the Toulmin model; framing and audience analysis.
objectives: Use ethos/pathos/logos deliberately and honestly
Structure an argument with the Toulmin model
Analyze an audience before persuading it
Distinguish persuasion from manipulation

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The honest craft of moving people with reasons.
- **ethos** — the speaker's credibility (Aristotle's *Rhetoric*, 4th c. BCE).
- **pathos** — the audience's emotions.
- **logos** — the argument's logic. Technical audiences over-invest in logos and starve the other two — but a correct argument from an untrusted speaker, framed without regard for stakes, still loses. All three are legitimate; the vice is substituting one for another.
- **Toulmin model** — Stephen Toulmin (1958): arguments have **claims**, **grounds** (evidence), **warrants** (the inference license connecting grounds to claim), **backing** (support for the warrant), **qualifiers**, and **rebuttals**.
- **the warrant insight** — in engineering reviews, fights are usually about *warrants* ("load tests predict production") — not about the data. Name the warrant and the debate gets productive.
- **audience analysis** — persuasion starts with the audience's **values, knowledge, and decision criteria** — not your material.
- **framing** — selecting which aspects of a situation are salient: the same migration is "risk reduction" to ops and "feature velocity" to product. Honest framing foregrounds relevant aspects; dishonest framing hides them.
- **persuasion vs. manipulation** — the line: persuasion respects the audience's rational agency — reasons they could endorse on reflection. Manipulation bypasses it: hidden agendas, manufactured urgency, selective data. The test you'd apply to others' decks, apply to your own: would this argument survive the audience knowing everything I know?

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Build a Toulmin brief for a proposal you actually care about.
1. **State your claim** in one sentence.
2. **List your grounds** — the evidence, no adjectives.
3. **Name the warrant** — why do these grounds support this claim? Write the inference license explicitly.
4. **Add backing, qualifier, rebuttal.** What supports the warrant? How strong is the claim, exactly? What is the best objection, steel-manned?
5. **Analyze the audience.** Values, knowledge, decision criteria — in their terms.
6. **Choose your appeals.** Where does this audience need ethos (why trust you), pathos (what's at stake for them), logos (the argument)?
7. **Frame honestly.** Foreground the aspects relevant to *their* decision — and include the trade-off you'd rather hide. Run the full-disclosure test.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a five-minute pitch, on paper.** Write the pitch for a technical proposal to a mixed audience (engineers, a manager, one executive): stakes first, options with trade-offs, recommendation with reasons. Attach a one-page Toulmin appendix — claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal. If the appendix and the pitch disagree, the appendix wins: fix the pitch.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, where do engineering debates usually break down — and why isn't it the data?
- Give Noah a claim — "load tests predict production behavior" — and ask: is that grounds or warrant?
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to map one of your past debates onto Toulmin's six boxes, then point to the box where it actually broke."
- *Honesty:* run the full-disclosure test on your own pitch before you present it — the manipulation check applies to you first.

cards.front: Aristotle's three appeals?
cards.back: Ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion), logos (logic) — Rhetoric, 4th c. BCE.

cards.front: Toulmin model components?
cards.back: Claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal (1958).

cards.front: In engineering debates, what do people usually fight about?
cards.back: Warrants — the inference licenses ('load tests predict prod'), not the raw data.

cards.front: Persuasion vs manipulation: the test?
cards.back: Does it respect rational agency? Would the argument survive full disclosure?

cards.front: What is framing?
cards.back: Selecting which aspects of a situation are salient for an audience — honest when it foregrounds relevant aspects.

cards.front: Logos, pathos, ethos in an engineering proposal — one example each.
cards.back: Logos: the benchmark table and cost model. Pathos: the 3 AM incident narrative that makes the cost real. Ethos: your team's record shipping this class of system. Aristotle's point: persuasion needs all three; engineers who bring only logos lose to those who bring the full set. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is the 'steelman', and how does it differ from the straw man?
cards.back: The straw man restates the opponent's position weakly to defeat it easily. The steelman restates it at its strongest — the version its best defender would endorse — and engages that. Steel-manning is the operational form of the principle of charity from Module 1. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Kairos: definition and a technical example.
cards.back: Kairos: the opportune moment — saying the right thing at the time it can be heard. Technical example: proposing the refactor right after the incident review, when the cost of the current design is vivid, rather than in a quiet quarter when it reads as gold-plating. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Citing your team's incident-free record to support a proposal appeals to:
quiz.explain: Credibility of the speaker — ethos. (See 'Concepts': ethos.)

quiz.q: In Toulmin's model, the warrant is:
choices: The inference license from grounds to claim
quiz.explain: The warrant is *why* the grounds support the claim — usually the contested part. (See 'Concepts': Toulmin model.)

quiz.q: Presenting only the metrics that favor your proposal is:
quiz.explain: Bypassing rational agency with selective evidence — manipulation, not persuasion. (See 'Concepts': persuasion vs. manipulation.)

quiz.q: Before persuading, first analyze the audience's:
quiz.explain: Persuasion starts from where the audience is, not from your slides. (See 'Concepts': audience analysis.)

quiz.q: 'Nine out of ten SRE teams use this pattern' appeals primarily to:
choices: Ethos, via social proof and authority
quiz.explain: Social-proof statistics borrow credibility from the crowd — an ethos move, legitimate when the crowd is relevant, fallacious when it substitutes for evidence. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A rebuttal that only names the fallacy ('that's a straw man') is incomplete because:
choices: Naming doesn't show what the argument actually establishes or where it fails
