quiz.explain: The label is a pointer, not an argument — you must still show the misrepresentation and what follows without it. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: In Toulmin's model, 'backing' supports the:
quiz.explain: Backing is the evidence or authority behind the warrant — the reason the inference rule itself is trustworthy. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The most reliable sign you're arguing about definitions rather than facts:
choices: The dispute dissolves when you substitute each side's definition — 'it depends what you mean by X'
quiz.explain: If restating with explicit definitions ends the fight, it was never about the world — it was about the words. Define terms first. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Economics for Engineers I — Markets & Costs
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 11. I'm your instructor. Economics for engineers, part one: markets and costs — supply and demand, opportunity cost, marginal thinking, and the cost structures inside every build-vs-buy and scale decision. We work it with numbers, not vibes.
objectives: Read a supply-demand diagram and predict price changes
Apply opportunity cost and marginal analysis
Distinguish fixed, variable, and sunk costs
Evaluate build-vs-buy with total cost of ownership

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The economics inside every build-vs-buy and scale decision.
- **demand** — slopes down: higher price → less wanted. **Supply** — slopes up. **Equilibrium** — where they cross: the market-clearing price and quantity.
- **shifts** — demand shifts with tastes, income, substitutes; supply shifts with input costs, technology, number of sellers. A demand shift moves price *and* quantity; a supply shift does the same in the opposite direction.
- **price ceiling** — set below equilibrium, creates a **shortage**; **price floor** — set above, creates a **surplus**.
- **opportunity cost** — the value of the best forgone alternative: the true cost of any choice.
- **marginal analysis** — decide at the margin: is the *next* unit's benefit worth its *next* unit's cost? "We've already spent $2M" is irrelevant to whether the next $100K is worth it.
- **fixed costs** — don't vary with output (the data center lease). **Variable costs** — do (per-request compute).
- **sunk costs** — spent and unrecoverable; rational decisions ignore them.
- **economies of scale** — average cost falls as output rises (high fixed, low marginal cost — the software business in one phrase).
- **total cost of ownership** — license + integration + operations + the opportunity cost of the engineers building it instead of the product. Buying looks expensive and building looks free because salaries are already budgeted — that is the opportunity-cost illusion. Decide on TCO over the realistic lifetime, including maintenance you will definitely pay.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Estimate a build-vs-buy TCO — worked example with illustrative numbers; substitute your own figures.
1. **State the decision and the lifetime.** "Build the billing service vs. buy a SaaS billing product; 3-year horizon."
2. **Price the build.** 2 engineers × 3 months × $20k loaded cost/month = $120k to build. Maintenance: 0.25 engineer/year × $240k = $60k/year → $180k over 3 years. Build cash subtotal: $300k.
3. **Price the buy.** $4k/month license = $144k over 3 years. Integration: 1 engineer × 1 month = $20k. Ops overhead: $10k/year = $30k. Buy subtotal: $194k.
4. **Add the opportunity cost — this is the correction.** The build consumes 6 engineer-months that are already budgeted, which is exactly the illusion: the real cost is the product work forgone. (Illustrative: had those months shipped the checkout revamp worth ~$200k in margin, the build's true economic cost is $300k cash + $200k forgone = $500k.)
5. **Decide at the margin.** Compare forward-looking totals only — $500k vs. $194k at current scale. Any prototype spend to date is sunk: exclude it.
6. **Stress-test at scale.** At 10× usage the SaaS fees scale with volume while the build has near-zero marginal cost — economies of scale can flip the answer. Recompute at 3× and 10× before deciding.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a build-vs-buy decision memo.** Take a real decision on your roadmap. Compute TCO over the realistic lifetime — license/fees + integration + operations + opportunity cost of diverted engineers + maintenance. Name the sunk-cost fallacy explicitly if past spend is invoked. Decide on forward-looking numbers, stress-test at 3× scale, and land a recommendation.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, why do rational decisions ignore sunk costs?
- Give Noah two figures and ask for the classification: (a) the data-center lease, (b) the $2M already spent on a failing project.
- *Worked check:* "Ask Noah to walk your current build-vs-buy line by line — cash costs, opportunity cost, sunk exclusions — and find the line you'd rather hide."
- *Honesty:* the numbers in the worked estimation are illustrative — your memo must use your real figures, sourced, with the uncertainty stated.

cards.front: What shifts demand vs supply?
cards.back: Demand: tastes, income, substitutes. Supply: input costs, technology, number of sellers.

cards.front: Opportunity cost?
cards.back: The value of the best alternative you give up — the true cost of a choice.

cards.front: Why do rational decisions ignore sunk costs?
cards.back: They're unrecoverable; only future costs and benefits should decide.

cards.front: Economies of scale in one phrase?
cards.back: Average cost falls as output rises — high fixed, low marginal cost.

cards.front: The build-vs-buy illusion?
cards.back: Building looks free because salaries are sunk-budgeted; TCO must include opportunity cost + maintenance.

cards.front: Define marginal cost, with the cloud example from the module.
cards.back: Marginal cost: the cost of one more unit. Cloud example: the marginal cost of serving one more API request is near zero (electricity plus a sliver of capacity), while the average cost includes the data center — which is why usage-based pricing can look like magic and still be rational. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Price elasticity: definition and why it matters for SaaS pricing.
cards.back: Elasticity: how much quantity demanded responds to price changes. Inelastic demand (life-critical tooling) tolerates price rises; elastic demand (nice-to-have dashboards) punishes them. SaaS tiers are elasticity engineering — charge the inelastic segment more, keep the elastic segment in the funnel. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is a 'Veblen good', and does software have any?
cards.back: A good whose demand rises with price because price signals status. Pure software rarely qualifies — but enterprise software with 'nobody got fired for buying it' dynamics rhymes with it: the high price is part of the risk story being purchased. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A price ceiling set below equilibrium causes:
quiz.explain: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the capped price. (See 'Concepts': price ceiling.)

quiz.q: $2M already spent on a failing project. The next phase costs $200K for $150K of value. Rational choice?
choices: Stop — the $2M is sunk; marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit
quiz.explain: Sunk costs are irrelevant; at the margin, $200K > $150K, so stop. (See 'Concepts': sunk costs; 'Worked estimation' step 5.)

quiz.q: Software has high fixed and near-zero marginal cost, so it exhibits:
quiz.explain: Average cost collapses as users grow — the economics of the whole industry. (See 'Concepts': economies of scale.)

quiz.q: A new GPU generation halves training cost. In supply-demand terms:
choices: Supply shifts right; price falls, quantity rises
quiz.explain: Lower input cost shifts supply right — the standard supply-shock result. (See 'Concepts': shifts.)

quiz.q: A team keeps a failing tool because 'we already paid for the license.' This is:
quiz.explain: Past spending is unrecoverable; only future costs and benefits should decide. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: If demand is inelastic, a price increase will:
quiz.explain: Quantity falls proportionally less than price rises, so revenue (P×Q) grows. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The 'build-vs-buy illusion' is that teams compare:
choices: Build cost to buy price, ignoring maintenance, opportunity cost, and the buy option's roadmap
quiz.explain: Build estimates omit the long tail — maintenance, on-call, and the foregone roadmap — while buy prices are quoted all-in. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A per-seat license for a tool used five minutes a day is best analyzed via:
choices: Cost per unit of value delivered, not sticker price
quiz.explain: Normalize to the value unit — cost per incident avoided, per deploy, per hour saved — before comparing options. (Hands-on procedure.)

modules.title: Economics for Engineers II — Incentives & Games
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 12. I'm your instructor. Part two: incentives and games — externalities, public goods, the prisoner's dilemma, Nash equilibria, and mechanism design. Why systems behave the way they do once humans are in the loop — and how to design the loop.
objectives: Identify externalities and public-goods problems
Find Nash equilibria in 2×2 games
Explain the prisoner's dilemma and its escapes
Design incentives instead of wishing for cooperation

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Why systems behave the way they do once humans are in the loop.
- **externality** — a cost or benefit imposed on third parties: pollution (negative), open-source software (positive).
- **public good** — non-excludable and non-rivalrous (clean air, basic research): everyone benefits, nobody wants to pay.
- **free-rider problem** — why public goods are under-provided.
- **the fixes** — price the externality (taxes, cap-and-trade), assign property rights (Coase), or fund publicly.
- **game** — players, strategies, payoffs.
- **Nash equilibrium** — a strategy profile where no player can *unilaterally* do better; stable, not necessarily good.
- **working tools** — dominant strategies, best responses, backward induction (in sequential games). Model the incentives before predicting the behavior.
- **prisoner's dilemma** — payoffs make mutual defection the Nash equilibrium even though mutual cooperation pays both more: the canonical model of arms races, price wars, and feature-copying.
- **escapes** — **repetition** (tit-for-tat sustains cooperation), **contracts** with enforcement, **reputation** systems, and changing the payoffs themselves.
- **mechanism design** — reverse game theory: choose the rules so that self-interested play produces the outcome you want — auctions, congestion pricing, on-call rotations, bug bounties. The engineer's version: don't exhort people to cooperate; **design the payoff matrix** so cooperation is the equilibrium.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Solve a 2×2 game — the prisoner's dilemma, worked step by step. Payoffs below are illustrative (years in prison; lower is better). Rows are your strategies, columns are theirs; each cell is (your payoff, their payoff).
1. **Find your best responses.** If they cooperate: defecting gives 0 vs. −1 for cooperating — defect. If they defect: defecting gives −2 vs. −3 — defect. Defection is your dominant strategy.
2. **Mirror it.** Their reasoning is symmetric — defection dominates for them too.
3. **Mark the Nash equilibrium.** (Defect, Defect) at (−2, −2): neither player gains by unilaterally deviating.
4. **Compare to the optimum.** (Cooperate, Cooperate) at (−1, −1) pays both more — the equilibrium is stable *and* worse. That gap is the tragedy.
5. **Design the escape.** Repeat the game (tit-for-tat: retaliation makes defection unprofitable over time), add an enforceable contract, build reputation tracking — or change the payoffs themselves. Pick one and say why it fits your case.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: an incentive redesign.** Pick a cooperation failure on your team — on-call burden, code review latency, documentation debt. Model it as a game: players, strategies, payoffs. Find the Nash equilibrium and show why the bad outcome is stable. Then redesign the mechanism — rotate the burden, price the externality, add reputation — so cooperation becomes the equilibrium. One page of analysis, one page of proposed rules.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what is a Nash equilibrium — and why isn't it the same as the best outcome?
- Give Noah two mechanisms and ask what each prices or changes: congestion pricing, a bug bounty.
- *Worked check:* "Ask Noah to check your 2×2 solution — best responses, equilibrium, optimum — then to steel-man the case for defecting anyway."
- *Honesty:* the payoff numbers are illustrative scaffolding — your redesign must model your team's real incentives, observed, not assumed.

cards.front: Externality? Public good? Free-rider problem?
cards.back: Externality: third-party cost/benefit. Public good: non-excludable, non-rivalrous. Free-rider: benefit without paying.

cards.front: Nash equilibrium?
cards.back: A profile where no player gains by unilaterally deviating — stable, not necessarily good.

cards.front: Prisoner's dilemma: equilibrium vs optimum?
cards.back: Mutual defection is the Nash equilibrium; mutual cooperation pays more — the tragedy.

cards.front: Three escapes from the dilemma?
cards.back: Repetition (tit-for-tat), enforceable contracts, reputation — or change the payoffs.

cards.front: Mechanism design in one line?
cards.back: Choose the rules so self-interested play yields the outcome you want.

cards.front: Define 'tragedy of the commons' and give the engineering version.
cards.back: Shared resources get overused because each user captures the benefit and spreads the cost: the overgrazed pasture. Engineering version: the shared staging environment everyone 'just quickly' deploys to — individually rational, collectively broken. Fixes: pricing, quotas, norms, or ownership. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Signaling theory in one paragraph.
cards.back: When quality is unobservable, agents send costly signals to prove it: the peacock's tail, the rigorous certification, the open-source portfolio. The signal works because it is expensive to fake — cheap signals (self-awarded badges) carry no information. Applies to hiring, vendors, and credentials alike. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is 'Goodhart's law', and its metric-design implication?
cards.back: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' Teams optimize the metric, not the goal: ticket counts reward ticket-splitting. Implication: use metrics as diagnostics alongside judgment, rotate them, and never let one number own compensation. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A factory's smoke harms neighbors. This is a:
quiz.explain: A cost imposed on third parties outside the transaction. (See 'Concepts': externality.)

quiz.q: In the prisoner's dilemma, the Nash equilibrium is:
quiz.explain: Each player gains by defecting regardless of the other's move — defection dominates. (See 'Concepts': prisoner's dilemma; 'Worked estimation' steps 1–3.)

quiz.q: Tit-for-tat sustains cooperation in repeated games because:
choices: Retaliation makes defection unprofitable over time
quiz.explain: The shadow of future retaliation shifts the equilibrium toward cooperation. (See 'Concepts': escapes.)

quiz.q: Congestion pricing on a highway is an example of:
quiz.explain: It charges drivers the congestion cost they impose — designing the payoff matrix. (See 'Concepts': mechanism design.)

quiz.q: Two vendors both cut prices until neither profits. This is the logic of:
choices: A Nash equilibrium that is not Pareto-optimal
Both — the price war is a prisoner's dilemma whose Nash equilibrium leaves both worse off
quiz.explain: Each cuts prices as a best response (Nash), yet both would prefer mutual restraint — which is not an equilibrium without enforcement. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A team adopts an on-call rotation nobody wants but everyone endures. The stable-but-suboptimal outcome is an example of:
quiz.explain: No individual can profitably deviate alone — the equilibrium holds even though all would prefer a coordinated alternative. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Paying engineers per line of code is a textbook case of:
quiz.explain: The measure becomes the target: verbose code, copied blocks — the metric degrades exactly because it is rewarded. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A carbon tax on compute is, in mechanism-design terms:
choices: Internalizing a negative externality by pricing it
quiz.explain: The tax makes the private cost reflect the social cost, aligning incentives with the efficient outcome — like congestion pricing in the module. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Law & Policy Literacy
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 13. I'm your instructor. Law and policy literacy: intellectual property, liability, privacy regulation, and how policy actually gets made. What every technologist should know — without pretending to be a lawyer.
objectives: Distinguish copyright, patent, trademark, and trade secret
Describe how software liability generally works
Name the major privacy regimes and their logic
Explain how technical standards become policy

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Read law and policy as a literate citizen — orientation, not counsel.
- **copyright** — protects expression (code, text); automatic on creation; long terms. Open-source licenses (MIT, GPL) are copyright licenses granting permissions.
- **patent** — protects inventions; requires application and disclosure; ~20-year terms; software patentability varies by jurisdiction.
- **trademark** — protects brand identifiers.
- **trade secret** — protected by secrecy itself.
- **literacy, not legal advice** — consult counsel for real decisions.
- **liability** — software has historically faced limited liability for defects: licenses disclaim warranties, and courts treat software as a service as much as a product. That settlement is under pressure: critical infrastructure, autonomous systems, and AI are pushing toward product-like liability. The direction matters for design: **document** safety reasoning as if a court will read it, because one might.
- **GDPR** (EU, 2018) — consent, data minimization, purpose limitation, the right to erasure, heavy fines; reshaped global practice.
- **CCPA/CPRA** (California) — opt-out of sale/sharing, deletion rights.
- **sectoral US law** — health (HIPAA), children (COPPA).
- **the common logic** — individuals get rights over their data; collectors get obligations. Design for data minimization from the start.
- **how policy gets made** — **legislation**, **regulation** (agencies writing rules under statutes), **standards** (IETF, W3C, NIST — often voluntary until referenced by law), and **litigation**. Technologists influence all four: writing standards, commenting on rulemakings, and — most powerfully — building the systems whose properties the law then assumes. Code is policy's raw material.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Read a license like a literate citizen — do this on a dependency you actually ship.
1. **Pick a dependency** your project ships — open its license file.
2. **Identify the grant.** What permissions does the copyright holder give you, exactly?
3. **Identify the conditions.** What must you do in return (attribution, source disclosure, same-license)?
4. **Read the warranty disclaimer.** Note what the licensor disclaims — then ask who bears the risk that remains.
5. **Map it to your use.** Are you compliant as you distribute today — including in containers, SaaS, and vendored copies?
6. **Know the handoff.** Write down the fact pattern that would make you call counsel instead of deciding yourself — and keep that note with the license.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a policy-impact memo.** For a system you build or plan: (a) which IP regimes touch it (your code, your brand, your dependencies' licenses), (b) which privacy regimes apply to its data and what obligations follow, (c) the liability direction and what safety reasoning you'd document today, (d) one standards body or rulemaking where your team's input would matter. Header on every page: literacy, not legal advice.

- Give Noah two artifacts and ask for the IP read: (a) your codebase, (b) your product's name.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to map the four policymaking channels — legislation, regulation, standards, litigation — onto one technology you follow, with a real example in each box."
- *Honesty:* this module is orientation, not counsel — Noah will remind you: for real decisions, consult a lawyer.

cards.front: Copyright vs patent vs trademark vs trade secret?
cards.back: Copyright: expression, automatic. Patent: inventions, applied for, ~20yr. Trademark: brand marks. Trade secret: protected by secrecy.

cards.front: GDPR's core principles?
cards.back: Consent, data minimization, purpose limitation, erasure rights, accountability — EU, 2018.

cards.front: Why does software liability matter more now?
cards.back: Critical infrastructure, autonomous systems, AI are pushing software toward product-like liability.

cards.front: Four channels of policymaking?
cards.back: Legislation, agency regulation, technical standards, litigation.

cards.front: The engineer's policy move?
cards.back: Design for data minimization; document safety reasoning; engage standards and rulemakings.

cards.front: Fair use: the four factors, briefly.
cards.back: (1) Purpose and character of use (commercial vs. transformative), (2) nature of the copyrighted work, (3) amount and substantiality taken, (4) effect on the market for the original. Training-data debates turn on factor 1 (is training transformative?) and factor 4 (does it substitute for the work?). (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is the 'right to be forgotten', and its engineering cost?
cards.back: The EU-derived right to have personal data erased from search results and systems under conditions. Engineering cost: deletion must propagate through backups, caches, logs, and ML training sets — 'delete' becomes a distributed-systems problem. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Section 230 in one paragraph — what it does and doesn't do.
cards.back: US law shielding platforms from liability for user-posted content while letting them moderate it — the legal basis of the modern social web. It doesn't shield federal crimes, IP claims, or (since 2018) sex trafficking; and its future is the most litigated policy question in tech law. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: An open-source license (e.g., MIT) is legally:
quiz.explain: Copyright vests automatically; the license is the author's permission slip with conditions. (See 'Concepts': copyright.)

quiz.q: GDPR's data minimization principle requires:
choices: Collecting only data needed for the stated purpose
Storing data only in the EU
quiz.explain: Purpose limitation + minimization: collect what the purpose needs, nothing more. (See 'Concepts': GDPR.)

quiz.q: Technical standards (IETF, NIST) become binding when:
choices: Referenced by law, contract, or procurement
quiz.explain: Standards are voluntary until legislation, regulation, or contracts incorporate them. (See 'Concepts': how policy gets made.)

quiz.q: This module's stance on legal questions is:
choices: Literacy only — consult counsel for real decisions
quiz.explain: Stated throughout: this is orientation, not counsel. (See 'Noah check-in': honesty.)

quiz.q: A patent protects:
choices: Novel, non-obvious, useful inventions — for about 20 years
quiz.explain: Patents cover inventions (not expression — that's copyright; not brands — trademark; not secrets — trade secret). (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Releasing code under the MIT license means:
choices: Anyone can do almost anything with it, including in proprietary products, with attribution
quiz.explain: MIT is permissive: use, modify, sell — keep the copyright notice. Copyleft (GPL) would require sharing derivatives. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Under GDPR, the lawful basis most startups actually rely on for product analytics is usually:
choices: Legitimate interests, documented via a balancing test
quiz.explain: Consent is brittle (must be freely given, revocable); most analytics runs on documented legitimate interests with opt-outs. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: An NDA's core function is to:
choices: Create a contractual duty of confidentiality around disclosed information
quiz.explain: NDAs don't stop independent discovery or competition — they make the disclosed information legally protected as between the parties. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Synthesis — The Technologist as Citizen
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 14 — the capstone. I'm your instructor, and this is where the thirteen modules fuse: philosophy, history, writing, rhetoric, economics, and law combining in the judgment of a senior technologist. You'll run one case through all six lenses, and leave with a practice rather than a credential — because this course confers none.
objectives: Integrate the humanities lenses on a single case
Write a reasoned position on a technology policy question
Argue a technical decision to a non-technical audience
Maintain a personal learning practice in the humanities

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The integration — every lens, one judgment.
- **the six lenses** — ethics (duties vs. outcomes), epistemology (what do the accuracy claims actually establish, on what data?), history (which past expansions are the precedent?), economics (who bears the costs, who captures the gains?), law (which regimes govern the data and the deployment?), rhetoric (how do you argue the decision to the people affected?).
- **the worked case** — deploying facial recognition for building access, run through all six: duties to subjects vs. aggregate safety; the evidence behind the accuracy claims; surveillance-expansion precedents; cost/gain distribution; biometric data regimes; the argument to the people scanned.
- **senior judgment** — not deeper technical knowledge but wider **context**: second-order effects, stakeholder legitimacy, reversibility, and the ability to say "we should not build this" — with reasons. The humanities are the training ground for thinking about ends, not just means.
- **arguing to non-technical audiences** — translate without condescending: lead with **stakes** (what changes for them), then **options** with trade-offs, then your **recommendation** with reasons. Drop jargon or define it once. Expect values questions — "is this fair?" — and answer them as values questions, not technical puzzles.
- **a personal practice** — the course ends; the practice doesn't. Read one serious book a quarter outside your field. Write — memos, essays, reading notes — because writing is thinking. Argue with people who disagree with you, charitably. The goal is not to become a philosopher but to become a technologist whose judgment deserves trust.
- **the through-line** — structured reasoning about human ends and means: each area of this course is a discipline of thinking about what matters and why, in service of better building.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the six-lens review on a live decision — a deployment, a data collection, a model launch.
1. **Pick a real decision** — something pending, with stakes.
2. **Ethics pass.** Duties and outcomes: who is used as a means, what are the aggregate effects?
3. **Epistemology pass.** What do the supporting claims actually establish? Falsifiable? Replicated?
4. **History pass.** What is the precedent — and did it end well?
5. **Economics pass.** Who bears the costs, who captures the gains? What are the incentives once deployed?
6. **Law pass.** Which regimes govern? What must you document?
7. **Rhetoric pass.** Draft the argument to the affected people: stakes, options, recommendation.
8. **Integrate.** No single lens decides — write the judgment that weighs them, including what you still don't know. That paragraph is the deliverable.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: the citizen's memo — the course capstone.** Write a reasoned position on a technology policy question (yours, or the facial-recognition case): all six lenses in their own sections, the integration paragraph, and a recommendation — including "do not build" if the lenses land there. Then set up the personal practice: pick next quarter's serious book, start the reading notes, and schedule the charitable argument. File the memo where your future self will find it.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what is judgment in this course's sense — and what is it not?
- Give Noah one case — facial recognition for building access — and ask for one question per lens.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to grade your capstone memo against the six lenses and tell you which lens is weakest — then strengthen it."
- *Honesty:* this course confers no certificate and no credential — what it offers is a practice. Ideas are paraphrased and attributed; nothing here is legal advice; the judgment, in the end, is yours.

cards.back: Wider context: second-order effects, legitimacy, reversibility — thinking about ends, not just means.

cards.front: A sustainable humanities practice?
cards.back: One serious book a quarter outside your field; write regularly; argue charitably with disagreeing minds.

cards.front: Name the six lenses and the question each asks of a deployment.
cards.back: Ethics: is it right (duties, outcomes)? Epistemology: what do the claims establish? History: what are the precedents? Economics: who bears costs and gains? Law: which regimes govern? Rhetoric: how do I argue it to those affected?

cards.front: What is the senior technologist's distinctive move, per this module?
cards.back: Saying 'we should not build this' — with reasons — from wider context: second-order effects, legitimacy, reversibility. Ends, not just means.

cards.front: The module's 'judgment' vs. 'knowledge' distinction?
cards.back: Knowledge is having the frameworks; judgment is choosing which framework the situation calls for, under uncertainty and time pressure. The course builds knowledge in every module; the synthesis builds judgment by forcing the lenses onto one live decision. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What does 'the technologist as citizen' demand, per the module?
cards.back: That technical skill be exercised inside civic responsibility: understanding the policy process, writing for non-technical audiences, pricing externalities, and accepting that deployed systems are social facts — not just code. Citizenship is the frame the whole course points at. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Judgment, as developed in this course, is best described as:
choices: The integration of multiple lenses on ends as well as means
quiz.explain: Judgment = structured thinking about what is worth doing, using every lens. (See 'Concepts': the through-line.)

quiz.q: When asked 'is this system fair?', the skilled response:
choices: Answer it as a values question with reasons
quiz.explain: Values questions deserve values reasoning — metrics alone dodge the question. (See 'Concepts': arguing to non-technical audiences.)

quiz.q: The through-line connecting all six humanities areas is:
choices: Structured reasoning about human ends and means
quiz.explain: Each area is a discipline of thinking about what matters and why — in service of better building. (See 'Concepts': the through-line.)

quiz.explain: Practice, not review: read widely, write to think, argue well. (See 'Concepts': a personal practice.)

quiz.q: A deployment decision analyzed through only the economics lens risks:
choices: Optimizing incentives and costs while missing ethical, epistemic, and political dimensions
quiz.explain: Single-lens analysis is precisely the failure mode the synthesis exists to prevent — each lens catches what the others miss. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The strongest structure for arguing a technical decision to non-technical stakeholders is:
choices: BLUF, stakes in their terms, evidence, explicit trade-offs, recommendation
A long history of the technology
quiz.explain: Lead with the conclusion, translate stakes into their currency, show the evidence, name the trade-offs honestly. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: 'Senior judgment' in this course means:
choices: Selecting the right lens under uncertainty, and being able to defend the choice
quiz.explain: Judgment is lens-selection plus defensibility — the synthesis module's definition. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The through-line of the course, in one claim:
choices: Every deployed system is simultaneously a technical, economic, ethical, and political artifact
quiz.explain: The course's thesis: ship systems with all four dimensions in view, because the world will evaluate them on all four regardless. (Concepts.)

scriptLabs.title: Argument mapping: dissect a live proposal
scriptLabs.brief: Take a real technical proposal — an RFC, a vendor pitch, or a design doc — and map its argument structure: claims, premises, warrants, backing, and rebuttals. Uses the Toulmin model from the Rhetoric module.
scriptLabs.starter:
# Argument map: <proposal title>
# 1. MAIN CLAIM (the conclusion being argued for):
# 2. PREMISES (numbered — what the claim rests on):
# 3. WARRANT (the inference rule connecting premises to claim):
# 4. BACKING (evidence that the warrant is trustworthy):
# 5. REBUTTAL (the strongest counter-argument, steel-manned):
# 6. VERDICT (valid? sound? what evidence would change your mind?):
scriptLabs.hint: The warrant is the step most proposals skip: WHY do these premises imply this claim? State it explicitly, then ask whether the backing actually supports it.
scriptLabs.solution:
# Argument map: Adopt Postgres for the billing service
# 1. MAIN CLAIM: Migrate billing from MySQL to Postgres in Q1.
# 2. PREMISES: (a) Billing needs serializable transactions across shards. (b) Our MySQL setup cannot do cross-shard serializable writes. (c) Postgres 16 handles our peak write load in benchmarks.
# 3. WARRANT: If the current store cannot meet a hard requirement and the candidate can, migration is justified.
# 4. BACKING: Benchmark report 2026-09 (appendix A); two incident postmortems citing the MySQL limitation.
# 5. REBUTTAL (steel-manned): Migration risk exceeds the benefit — the serializable requirement occurs in 0.1% of transactions, and application-level sagas would cover it without a database migration.
# 6. VERDICT: Valid form; soundness hinges on premise (a) — if the 0.1% figure is right, the warrant's 'hard requirement' framing fails. Request the transaction-mix data before deciding.

scriptLabs.title: Close reading: charity pass on a hard text
scriptLabs.brief: Perform a two-pass close reading of a short philosophical excerpt (the module suggests Mill on liberty or a passage from the course notes): first a charity pass reconstructing the strongest version of the argument, then a critical pass testing its premises.
scriptLabs.starter:
# Close reading: <text and passage>
# CHARITY PASS (strongest reconstruction):
# - The author's central claim, in your own words:
# - The premises, numbered, as the author would defend them:
# CRITICAL PASS:
# - PREMISES under pressure (which is weakest, and why):
# - OBJECTION (the best one-sentence objection):
# - CHARITABLE REPLY (how the author might answer it):
# VERDICT: what survives the critical pass?
scriptLabs.hint: Do the charity pass fully before any criticism — write the version of the argument the author's smartest defender would endorse. Only then attack. Reversing the order produces straw men.
scriptLabs.solution:
# Close reading: Mill, On Liberty, ch. 1 (harm principle passage)
# CHARITY PASS: The state (or society) may coerce an individual only to prevent harm to others; the individual's own good is never sufficient warrant. Premises: (1) human fallibility makes any censor likely wrong sometimes; (2) truth emerges from open contest; (3) individuality is a constitutive part of well-being, not a luxury.
# CRITICAL PASS: Premise (3) is the load-bearing one — a critic who denies that individuality matters can accept (1) and (2) and still regulate. OBJECTION: the harm principle under-determines cases like hate speech, where 'harm' itself is contested. CHARITABLE REPLY: Mill would distinguish offense from harm and demand the critic show concrete injury.
# VERDICT: the epistemic argument (fallibility + contest) survives even if you reject the individuality premise — it independently supports free expression.

scenarios.title: AI Deployment Ethics Review
scenarios.context: Your team built a resume-screening model. It is 12% more 'accurate' than human screeners on historical data, but an audit shows it downgrades resumes with employment gaps — disproportionately affecting caregivers returning to work. Leadership wants to ship Friday.

steps.prompt: How do you frame the decision?

options.text: Run the three-traditions analysis before deciding: duties, consequences, and character
options.why: The traditions structure the trade-off instead of letting urgency decide: deontology flags treating applicants as mere means, consequentialism weighs aggregate hiring gains vs. harms, virtue asks what a good craftsperson ships.

options.text: Ship it — 12% accuracy gain is the only metric that matters
options.why: Accuracy on biased historical data is not the same as a good hiring decision; the metric begs the question.

options.text: Kill the project quietly without analysis
options.why: Avoidance without reasoning teaches the org nothing and may forfeit real benefits a constrained deployment could capture.

steps.prompt: Analysis done. What do you recommend?

options.text: Constrained pilot: remove the gap-penalizing features, add human review of edge cases, instrument outcomes, revisit in 90 days
options.why: Collingridge-aware: reversible, monitored, humble. It captures value while containing the foreseeable harm — and generates the data a fuller decision needs.

options.text: Full deployment with a fairness statement on the website
options.why: A statement doesn't change the model's behavior; this is ethics theater.

options.text: Hand the decision to legal alone
options.why: Legal sets the floor, not the ceiling — 'lawful' and 'right' are different questions.

scenarios.title: The Dual-Use Dilemma
scenarios.context: Your open-source computer-vision library — built for wildlife conservation — is being forked for automated targeting in a conflict zone. Contributors are split: pull the repo, or keep shipping?

steps.prompt: First, how do you think about it?

options.text: Dual-use analysis: same mechanism, divergent uses — ask which uses, under what controls
options.why: Neither 'technology is neutral' nor 'ban everything' survives contact with the case; the serious question is always about specific uses and controls.

options.text: It's neutral — tools have no moral character
options.why: Affordances shape use; a targeting-ready vision stack is not morally identical to a spreadsheet.
Deletion also kills the conservation work and won't un-publish the forks — consequences matter too.

steps.prompt: What concrete step best fits the analysis?

options.text: Keep the conservation core open; gate the targeting-enabling modules behind review, document foreseeable misuse, add a use policy
options.why: Differentiated controls: preserve the benign use, add friction to the harmful one, document the reasoning — the engineer's four moves.

options.text: Do nothing — open source means no control
options.why: License terms, module structure, and documentation are all levers; 'no control' is false.
Deception violates professional duties and destroys the trust the conservation work depends on.

scenarios.title: Writing Under Pressure
scenarios.context: A Sev-1 outage just ended. You must write the incident review: it will be read by engineers, executives, and possibly a customer. The root cause implicates a shortcut your own team took.

options.text: BLUF: impact and resolution first, then timeline, root cause (honest), action items with owners
options.why: Scanners get the essentials in paragraph one; the honest root cause preserves credibility; owned actions make it a tool, not a ritual.

options.text: Chronological narrative from the first alert
options.why: Chronology buries the conclusion; busy readers never reach the decisions.

options.text: Emphasize external factors to protect the team
options.why: Selective framing is manipulation; blameless review requires honest causation — blame the system, describe it truthfully.

steps.prompt: How do you phrase the team's shortcut?

options.text: State it plainly with the reasoning at the time, then the systemic fix that removes the temptation
options.why: Honest, blameless, and forward-looking: it names the cause without personal attack and fixes the incentive.

options.text: Omit it — the fix is what matters
options.why: Omitting known causation corrupts the record and guarantees recurrence.

options.text: Name and shame the engineer who took it
options.why: Blame ends learning; the next shortcut will just be hidden better.

choices: A decision oracle for hard cases
A floor and shared language for escalation

mockTasks.q: A theory compatible with every possible observation is, for Popper:
mockTasks.explain: Falsifiability is the demarcation line: no forbidden observations, no science.

choices: Justified true belief can be accidentally true

mockTasks.q: In Kuhn's account, a paradigm determines:

mockTasks.explain: Epicycles were structurally wrong but predicted planetary positions well — a lesson in prediction vs. truth.

mockTasks.q: The word 'algorithm' derives from:
mockTasks.explain: The 9th-century scholar's name, Latinized, attached to his systematic procedures.

mockTasks.q: Galileo's 1633 condemnation concerned:
mockTasks.explain: The Inquisition's trial centered on his defense of the Copernican system.

mockTasks.q: Kepler derived his laws primarily from:
mockTasks.explain: Brahe's unprecedentedly precise naked-eye data made the ellipses detectable.

mockTasks.q: Maxwell's equations unified:
mockTasks.explain: One framework for electric and magnetic fields, with light as an electromagnetic wave.

mockTasks.q: Hertz's 1887 experiments confirmed:
mockTasks.explain: Hertz generated and detected radio waves — the waves Maxwell's theory required.

mockTasks.q: Turing's 1936 paper established:
choices: The theoretical model of universal computation
mockTasks.explain: The universal Turing machine defined computability before electronic computers existed.

mockTasks.q: The transistor (1947) rested on which science?
mockTasks.explain: Band theory and semiconductor physics are quantum-mechanical — 1920s theory, 1940s device.

mockTasks.q: The Second Industrial Revolution is associated with:
mockTasks.explain: ~1870–1914: electrification, Bessemer steel, chemical industry, internal combustion.

mockTasks.q: Moore's 'chasm' lies between:
choices: Early adopters and the early majority
mockTasks.explain: Crossing from enthusiasts to the pragmatic majority is the go-to-market crux.

mockTasks.q: A disruptive technology, in Christensen's sense, typically starts:
choices: Worse and cheaper, serving overlooked customers
mockTasks.explain: Disruption enters low-end or new markets, then moves up as performance improves.

mockTasks.q: TCP/IP standardization (1983) mattered because:
choices: It created a common open layer enabling the internet's growth
mockTasks.explain: An open, shared protocol layer let diverse networks interoperate — infrastructure for everything above.

mockTasks.q: Which sentence is strongest?
choices: The service is restarted by the script.
The deploy script restarts the service.
It is important to note the service gets restarted.
mockTasks.explain: Concrete subject, active verb, no throat-clearing.

mockTasks.q: BLUF means:
mockTasks.explain: Lead with the conclusion so scanners can triage.

mockTasks.q: A runbook is tested by:
choices: Someone who didn't write it, during calm
mockTasks.explain: Only a fresh reader proves the runbook is self-sufficient; never first-test it in a real incident.

mockTasks.q: 'Latency got much worse' should become:
mockTasks.explain: Numbers beat adjectives — precise, checkable, actionable.

mockTasks.q: Citing your team's incident-free record to support a proposal appeals to:
mockTasks.explain: Credibility of the speaker — ethos. (Module 10: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: In Toulmin's model, the warrant is:
choices: The inference license from grounds to claim
mockTasks.explain: The warrant is why the grounds support the claim — usually the contested part. (Module 10: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Presenting only the metrics that favor your proposal is:
mockTasks.explain: Bypassing rational agency with selective evidence — manipulation, not persuasion. (Module 10: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Framing the same migration as 'risk reduction' to ops and 'feature velocity' to product is an example of:
mockTasks.explain: Framing selects which aspects are salient for an audience — honest when it foregrounds relevant aspects. (Module 10: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: A price ceiling set below equilibrium causes:
mockTasks.explain: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the capped price. (Module 11: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: $2M already spent on a failing project. The next phase costs $200K for $150K of value. Rational choice?
choices: Stop — the $2M is sunk; marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit
mockTasks.explain: Sunk costs are irrelevant; at the margin, $200K > $150K, so stop. (Module 11: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Software has high fixed and near-zero marginal cost, so it exhibits:
mockTasks.explain: Average cost collapses as users grow — the economics of the whole industry. (Module 11: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: A new GPU generation halves training cost. In supply-demand terms:
choices: Supply shifts right; price falls, quantity rises
mockTasks.explain: Lower input cost shifts supply right — the standard supply-shock result. (Module 11: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: A factory's smoke harms neighbors. This is a:
mockTasks.explain: A cost imposed on third parties outside the transaction. (Module 12: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: In the prisoner's dilemma, the Nash equilibrium is:
mockTasks.explain: Each player gains by defecting regardless of the other's move — defection dominates. (Module 12: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Tit-for-tat sustains cooperation in repeated games because:
choices: Retaliation makes defection unprofitable over time
mockTasks.explain: The shadow of future retaliation shifts the equilibrium toward cooperation. (Module 12: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Congestion pricing on a highway is an example of:
mockTasks.explain: It charges drivers the congestion cost they impose — designing the payoff matrix. (Module 12: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: An open-source license (e.g., MIT) is legally:
mockTasks.explain: Copyright vests automatically; the license is the author's permission slip with conditions. (Module 13: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: GDPR's data minimization principle requires:
choices: Collecting only data needed for the stated purpose
Storing data only in the EU
mockTasks.explain: Purpose limitation + minimization: collect what the purpose needs, nothing more. (Module 13: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Technical standards (IETF, NIST) become binding when:
choices: Referenced by law, contract, or procurement
mockTasks.explain: Standards are voluntary until legislation, regulation, or contracts incorporate them. (Module 13: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: This module's stance on legal questions is:
choices: Literacy only — consult counsel for real decisions
mockTasks.explain: Stated throughout: this is orientation, not counsel. (Module 13: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Judgment, as developed in this course, is best described as:
choices: The integration of multiple lenses on ends as well as means
mockTasks.explain: Judgment = structured thinking about what is worth doing, using every lens. (Module 14: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: When asked 'is this system fair?', the skilled response:
choices: Answer it as a values question with reasons
mockTasks.explain: Values questions deserve values reasoning — metrics alone dodge the question. (Module 14: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: The through-line connecting all six humanities areas is:
choices: Structured reasoning about human ends and means
mockTasks.explain: Each area is a discipline of thinking about what matters and why — in service of better building. (Module 14: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Which habit best sustains humanities learning post-course?
choices: Regular reading, writing, and charitable disagreement
mockTasks.explain: Practice, not review: read widely, write to think, argue well. (Module 14: Concepts.)

blocks.body:
- Modus ponens: P→Q, P ⊢ Q
- Modus tollens: P→Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P
- Valid = form; sound = valid + true premises

- Ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, post hoc
- Appeal to authority, begging the question, slippery slope
- Name it, then give the substantive reply

- Claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal
- Fights are usually about warrants

- Virtue (Aristotle): what kind of person? Habits, character.
- Deontology (Kant): duty; universalizable maxims; persons as ends.
- Consequentialism (Bentham/Mill): maximize good outcomes.

- Collingridge: design reversible, anticipatory, humble
- Dual use: which uses, under what controls?
- Document misuse, add friction, instrument, preserve override

- BLUF; headings; short paragraphs
- Active voice, concrete subjects, numbers over adjectives
- Define terms; cut 20% on second pass

- Ethos, pathos, logos (Aristotle)
- Audience: values, knowledge, decision criteria
- Persuasion respects agency; manipulation bypasses it

- ~700 BCE: Babylonian astronomy, base-60 arithmetic
- ~300 BCE: Euclid's Elements — the axiomatic method
- 3rd c. BCE: Archimedes — buoyancy, levers, pi by polygons
- 2nd c. CE: Ptolemy's Almagest — epicycles (wrong, predictive)
- 8th–13th c.: Al-Khwarizmi (algebra → 'algorithm'), Ibn al-Haytham (optics)
- 1543: Copernicus — heliocentrism
- 1609–1619: Kepler's laws from Brahe's data
- 1609 / 1633: Galileo — telescope; house arrest
- 1687: Newton's Principia — motion + universal gravitation

- 1859: Darwin — natural selection
- 1860s: Maxwell unifies electricity, magnetism, light; Hertz confirms (1887)
- 1900: Planck quantizes energy
- 1905 / 1915: Einstein — special, then general relativity
- 1920s: quantum mechanics (Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Dirac)
- 1936: Turing — the universal machine
- 1948: Shannon — information theory
- 1945–1969: ENIAC, transistor, integrated circuits, ARPANET

- S-curve: slow uptake → explosive growth → saturation
- Chasm (Moore): early adopters → early majority
- Innovator's Dilemma (Christensen, 1997): disruption from below
- Kodak (1975, Sasson) invented the digital camera and lost
- Internet: ARPANET (1969) → TCP/IP (1983) → Web (1990–); open protocols won

- Opportunity cost: the best forgone alternative
- Marginal analysis: decide on the next unit
- Fixed vs variable vs sunk (sunk is ignored)
- TCO: license + integration + ops + opportunity cost + maintenance
- Price ceiling below equilibrium → shortage; floor above → surplus

- Nash equilibrium: no unilateral deviation pays
- Prisoner's dilemma: mutual defection stable, mutual cooperation better
- Escapes: repetition (tit-for-tat), contracts, reputation, new payoffs
- Mechanism design: set rules so self-interest yields the desired outcome
- Externality: third-party cost/benefit; price it, assign rights (Coase), or fund it

- Copyright: expression, automatic (MIT/GPL are copyright licenses)
- Patent: inventions, ~20yr; Trademark: brand marks; Trade secret: secrecy
- GDPR (EU, 2018): consent, minimization, purpose limitation, erasure
- CCPA/CPRA: opt-out of sale/sharing, deletion; HIPAA: health; COPPA: children
- Standards bind when referenced by law, contract, or procurement
- Literacy, not legal advice

answerBank.q: Argue for or against deploying a hiring model that is more accurate on average but disadvantages one group.
answerBank.a: Framework: (1) Epistemology — what does 'accurate' mean on biased labels? (2) Deontology — does it treat applicants as ends? (3) Consequentialism — aggregate gains vs. concentrated harms, including second-order effects on the applicant pool. (4) Reversibility — can the decision be undone and monitored? A defensible answer works all four and lands on a constrained, monitored pilot or a no-go with reasons — never on the metric alone.

answerBank.q: Is open-sourcing a powerful model dual-use? What follows?
answerBank.a: Framework: identify the mechanism's affordances for benign and harmful uses separately; assess how much the release *marginally* enables harm versus the status quo; consider controls (staged release, use policies, monitoring). 'Neutral' and 'ban it' are both evasions — the answer is always which uses under what controls, with the reasoning documented.

answerBank.q: Explain a technical trade-off to a non-technical executive.
answerBank.a: Framework: stakes first (what changes for them), options with honest trade-offs, recommendation with reasons. One defined term per jargon item, or none. End with the decision you need from them and by when. Anticipate the values question ('is it fair/safe?') and answer it as a values question.

answerBank.q: A paper claims a breakthrough. How do you read it as an epistemologist?
answerBank.a: Framework: Popper — what would falsify it? Kuhn — which paradigm does it extend or challenge? Replication — sample size, pre-registration, effect size with uncertainty, independent replication. Treat it as conjecture until the field converges; never cite the press release.

answerBank.q: Build vs. buy: make the economic case.
answerBank.a: Framework: total cost of ownership over the realistic lifetime — license/fees + integration + operations + opportunity cost of diverted engineers + maintenance. Compare marginal costs at expected scale. Name the sunk-cost fallacy explicitly if past spend is invoked. Decide on forward-looking numbers.

answerBank.q: Your team is split on a rewrite. How do you decide?
answerBank.a: Framework: Toulmin — surface the warrants ('rewrites always fail' vs. 'the debt is fatal'), not just the data. Economics — opportunity cost of the rewrite vs. incremental repair. History — second-system effect (Brooks) as a caution. Decide with a time-boxed spike that could falsify the rewrite case.

terminalSims.title: Logic CLI drill
terminalSims.brief: Practice propositional-logic checks and argument-form identification against a canned shell. Type 'help' to list commands.

commands.out:
check <form>   test an argument form for validity
forms          list the named forms
quiz           a random argument to classify

Example: check "if P then Q; P; therefore Q"

modus ponens      if P then Q; P; therefore Q            (valid)
modus tollens     if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P    (valid)
affirm consequent if P then Q; Q; therefore P            (INVALID)
deny antecedent   if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q    (INVALID)
disj syllogism    P or Q; not P; therefore Q             (valid)

commands.cmd: check "if P then Q; P; therefore Q"
commands.out: VALID — modus ponens. The conclusion follows necessarily.

commands.cmd: check "if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P"
commands.out: VALID — modus tollens. Denying the consequent is the safe move.

commands.cmd: check "if P then Q; Q; therefore P"
commands.out: INVALID — affirming the consequent. Q may hold for other reasons.

commands.cmd: check "if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q"
commands.out: INVALID — denying the antecedent. P is sufficient, not necessary.

Classify: 'The cache is stale or the CDN is down. The cache is fresh. Therefore the CDN is down.'
(Type your answer, then: check "P or Q; not P; therefore Q" to verify.)

commands.cmd: check "P or Q; not P; therefore Q"
commands.out: VALID — disjunctive syllogism. Eliminating one disjunct leaves the other.

terminalSims.title: Argument workshop CLI
terminalSims.brief: Map claims and premises, test validity, and steel-man positions from the command line. Type 'help' to list commands.

commands.out:
map <claim>      scaffold a Toulmin map for a claim
steelman <view>   prompt the steel-man procedure
fallacy <name>   definition + example of a named fallacy

Example: fallacy strawman

CLAIM: we should migrate to Postgres
GROUNDS:    (list your evidence)
WARRANT:    (why do these grounds imply the claim?)
BACKING:    (why trust the warrant?)
REBUTTAL:   (strongest counter-case)
QUALIFIER:  (how confident — probably, certainly, plausibly?)

Strongest version: deploys stay atomic, cross-service transactions vanish, debugging is one process, and team cognitive load drops.
Now answer THAT — not the weak version ('monoliths are old').

Straw man: restating the opponent's position weakly to defeat it easily.
Antidote: steel-man first (see: steelman).

Post hoc ergo propter hoc: 'after it, therefore because of it.'
The deploy preceded the outage — correlation is not yet causation; check the evidence chain.

Not a fallacy — the principle of charity: reconstruct the strongest version of a claim before evaluating it.
